name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota lawmakers explore options for limited regulation of AI
description: A new legislative committee is studying how other states approach regulating artificial intelligence and is considering what policy steps may be necessary in North Dakota ahead of next year’s legislative session.  Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, is chairing the committee and said the ultimate goal is to produce recommendations that are “practical, balance[...]
text:
Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, is the chair of the new legislative committee focused on artificial intelligence and data centers. The committee held its first meeting on July 15, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)A new legislative committee is studying how other states approach regulating artificial intelligence and is considering what policy steps may be necessary in North Dakota ahead of next year’s legislative session. 
Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, is chairing the committee and said the ultimate goal is to produce recommendations that are “practical, balanced, and focused on the long-term interests of the people of North Dakota.”
“We want to ensure that we take a North Dakota-first approach, one where innovation can thrive,” Warrey said. “But we’ve got to protect our citizens within reason and maintain public trust.”
The committee is not considering any specific legislation at this time. But throughout the presentations during the committee’s first meeting Wednesday, members expressed an interest in more information regarding requiring more transparency of AI use, how government oversight is being enacted elsewhere, AI’s role in education and attempts to safeguard children. 
Data center concerns dominate public comment for new legislative committee

Most states have passed legislation regulating AI in one form or another. The majority of it has been targeted in nature, according to a presentation by William Clark of the National Conference of State Legislatures. 
“Instead of focusing on more comprehensive approaches that apply to all developers and all employers, really focusing on specific industries or specific types of applications, like chatbots or particular environmental regulations or particular education uses,” Clark said. 
Some of the most common subjects of legislation include AI use in healthcare and education, required disclosures of AI use for transparency and restrictions on deep-fakes images, Clark said. 
Clark said multiple states are restricting the use of deep fakes for sexually explicit content, especially relating to child sexual abuse materials, amending campaign laws to require disclosure of AI use in ads and prohibiting the use of those ads too close to an election, and protecting an individual’s digital likeness. 
Some states have gone a step further and enacted what the NCSL considers comprehensive regulation of how artificial intelligence is used, including: 

Utah: Passed a law in 2024 that established liability for use of AI if it violates consumer protection laws and isn’t disclosed.
Texas: In 2025, began requiring the disclosure of AI use to consumers, prohibited certain uses of AI and invested the Attorney General’s Office with authority to enforce compliance.
California: In 2025, began requiring AI developers to submit risk assessments for significant harm, established whistleblower protections and created a system to report AI safety incidents.
Illinois: Passed the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act earlier this year. The law is similar to California’s and goes a step further by requiring annual third party audits of AI developers.
Colorado: In 2026, repealed a 2024 law and replaced it with an attempt to address concerns about using AI to automate consequential decisions using an individual’s personal data.

“If one of these automated decision-making models was used for maybe denying a health claim, and so a person under this bill has the right to review the data that was used in that decision, provide additional corrections if they believe there was some sort of erroneous data, and if there was,” Clark said of Colorado’s law. “Then to have that decision reviewed once again.”
Rep. Todd Porter, a Republican from Mandan, questioned whether some of the laws would hold up in court.
“When I look through the list, it seems like there’s a lot of fences that are being put up that are unenforceable fences,” Porter said.
Rep. Rodd Porter, R-Mandan, listens to testimony during a meeting of the Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee on July 15, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
North Dakota has passed its own legislation in recent years. One bill expanded the state’s child pornography law to include images created by artificial intelligence. Another required a disclaimer on any political communication or political advertisement created, entirely or in part, with artificial intelligence.
All of these state-level regulations could potentially be pre-empted by the federal government if Congress takes action. 
Congress has or will consider multiple frameworks of AI safety legislation, said Barrie Tabin, senior legislative director for NCSL. Those include attempts to implement protections for children and regulations on AI development. None of the proposals have been passed by both chambers of Congress yet.
“There is a lot of discussion. But nothing moving rapidly through both the House and the Senate,” Tabin said. 
One of the roadblocks to some of the child safety legislation at the federal level has been industry pushback on First Amendment grounds, Tabin said. A congressional proposal to place the “duty of care,” or responsibility to ensure a platform avoids foreseeable harm to children, on the shoulders of AI developers, has been controversial even as the broader topic of child safety is bipartisan, Tabin said. 
One member of the committee, Mark Hagerott, a former chancellor of the North Dakota University System who has expertise in AI, said it would be a “dangerous overreach” if the AI industry continued to push back against protections for children on First Amendment grounds. 
“We protect our children down to the bread they eat, the milk they drink,” Hagerott said. “It just seems this is not going to sustain itself politically.”
Mark Hagerott, a former chancellor of the North Dakota University System, introduces a speaker during a meeting of the Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee on July 15, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Tabin said states also have to consider President Donald Trump’s executive orders. Those executive orders have called for the federal government to implement a single AI policy for the whole country, urges Congress to preempt conflicting state laws and emphasize the need to regulate with a light touch.
Tabin said the White House has emphasized “a very light touch, innovator-friendly approach to regulation,” but with mechanisms like age verification and parental control safeguards to protect children.
She said there is concern the federal government may hold back a state’s share of $250 billion in discretionary grant funding, such as the $20 billion in broadband access funding that has yet to be distributed, if the Trump administration feels a state’s AI regulation conflicts with the federal government’s approach. 
Sen. Janne Myrdal, a Republican from Edinburg, called the threat of the federal government withholding that funding an “overreach,” and a violation of the part of the Bill of Rights that reserves powers for the state and the public which are not delegated to the federal government.
“It’s very frustrating to me that the 10th Amendment is being stomped on,” Myrdal said. “It’s quite disgusting.”
Tabin predicted any attempt to withhold discretionary funding from states would be met with a strong reaction by state attorneys general. 
“I think there would probably be an upheaval, an uproar across the country in all states if they tried to withhold some of these other discretionary, unrelated funds because of what they deem to be an onerous AI law,” Tabin said. 
The meeting room for a new legislative committee to study artificial intelligence and data centers was standing room only on July 15, 2026. More than 70 members of the public were in attendance. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Legislative Management Chair David Hogue, a Republican senator from Minot, initiated the committee’s creation. He said Wednesday the goal should not necessarily be to draft legislation but to study the subject before the session. 
“Artificial intelligence is changing so fast it’s hard to keep up with it,” Hogue said Wednesday. “We need to know what other states and the federal government are doing.”
The next meeting of the Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee is scheduled for Aug. 13. The location has not been set.
Warrey said he expects the committee to meet five times in total, three times in Bismarck and two field trips to other communities. 
The chairman also said the committee will accept written testimony. That typically is not the case for interim committees. The written submissions will be linked in the meeting minutes. 
Written testimony can be submitted to edohm@ndlegis.gov. If the testimony is received more than a week after a committee meeting, it will be included in the minutes of the next meeting instead.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: A victory for ‘the right to tell people what they do not want to hear’
description: “‘It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.’” That’s how federal judge Mark Walker began his 2022 injunction blocking enforcement of Ron DeSantis’ “Stop Woke Act” in Florida institutions of higher education. In case you don’t recognize the quotation, it’s from George Orwell’s “1984:” You know, the novel where […]
text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis promoted his "Stop Woke Act," restricting classroom instruction about racism and other systemic problems, in Wildwood on Dec. 15, 2021. (Screenshot via DeSantis' Facebook)“‘It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.’”
That’s how federal judge Mark Walker began his 2022 injunction blocking enforcement of Ron DeSantis’ “Stop Woke Act” in Florida institutions of higher education.
In case you don’t recognize the quotation, it’s from George Orwell’s “1984:” You know, the novel where the Ministry of Truth rewrites history and forbids free enquiry.
Certain words are banned; wrong thinking is punished. Even hearing about disfavored ideas is considered an attack on decency and order.
As defendant in the case, the State of Florida argued (apparently with a straight face) university professors have the right to free speech, sure, but only if the state approves of that speech.
The law forbade teaching anything that explores racial or gender injustice.
You weren’t allowed to say, given how we still struggle to overcome discrimination against minorities, women, and the disabled, that maybe diversity, equity and inclusion programs helped a lot of people; you must embrace color-blindness in all things (because we all know race doesn’t matter in America!); yet, woe betide you if you ever made a white person feel “guilt, anguish, or other forms of psychological distress because of actions, in which the person played no part, committed in the past by other members of the same race, color, national origin, or sex.”
Like many of us teaching in the state university system, the judge was unimpressed.
DeSantis and the legal team from his Ministry of Truth appealed up the food chain to the 11th Circuit, and what do you know?
They lost again.
‘Breathtaking assertion of power’ 
The majority opinion, by a Trump appointee, is unsparing.
Judge Britt C. Grant wrote, “If the First Amendment offers any boundary of protection at all for public university classrooms, this statute crosses it.”
She called the Stop Woke law “a breathtaking assertion of power to ban unpopular ideas from public discourse.”
Naturally, the governor pitched a little hissy fit, taking to social media to say, “State universities are funded by taxpayers and directed by elected officials and their appointees. The state has both a right and a responsibility to ensure instruction at these universities is consistent with the underlying mission and to exclude indoctrination and ideological agendas.”
He called the decision “judicial overreach.”
Let’s talk about gubernatorial overreach. Or, to put it another way, what is this guy’s problem with education?
Is he really that frightened of ideas?
If he and his education appointees are so convinced their positions — slavery had an upside, gender is 100% biological, capitalism is divinely ordained, a woman’s highest destiny is to be a mother, vaccines are unnecessary, climate change isn’t real — are valid, surely they’d welcome testing them with historical records, expert reports, and empirical evidence.
Facts, even.
Reading books by and about, say, gay people, teaching the history of Stonewall, or examining central Supreme Court decisions such as Obergefell v. Hodges, do not mean straight people will somehow become gay, any more than studying Shakespeare’s “Julius Caesar” will necessarily inspire you to assassinate any official you think has gotten too big for his britches.
Gender studies will not destroy heterosexuality; it’s simply a way to talk about the ways people understand who they are, how they present themselves, how other people see them.
Snowflakes
Universities are supposed to be where you encounter people who aren’t like you, unfamiliar, maybe upsetting, points of view, tricky topics, and ideas your parents don’t approve of.
Intellectual freedom means we should be able to discuss almost anything.
Yet the DeSantis administration act like snowflakes, hypersensitive, unwilling to contemplate anything outside their very white, very Christian, pathetically nationalist, bubble.
DeSantis is especially nervous America’s racial history, trying to outlaw “The 1619 Project,” a brilliant collection of writings about how the arrival of the first slaves on the Virginia shore has informed and shaped our country, shutting down or crippling African American Studies programs.
I guess white people are so used to considering themselves the “real” Americans who had all the good ideas, invented all the good stuff, and “built this country,” the reality that Africa is as central to our identity as Europe is scary.
The governor and his crew seem especially freaked out by the possibility students might encounter Critical Race Theory. Listening to them, you’d think CRT is to blame for everything from high gas prices to the common cold.
CRT is pretty simple: Race is socially constructed (not biological) and racism is not merely a product of individual bias (though that’s part of it) but embedded in our legal, educational, medical, and financial systems.
Say a white person and a Black person commit the same crime. It would make sense if they got the same sentence, right?
But in most cases the Black person will get a longer sentence.
‘The perfect villain’
The Kaiser Family Foundation, a nonpartisan health policy think tank, has repeatedly shown structural racism (conscious or not) in the medical profession means doctors and nurses misdiagnose Black, Latino, and members of other ethnic communities far more often than they do whites, and, unlike with white patients, tend to dismiss their pain.
Infant mortality among people of color is at least twice as high than it is for whites.
There’s nothing sinister or anti-American in acknowledging, as Justice Thurgood Marshall said, the original Constitution was “defective from the start,” given that it upheld slaveholders’ rights in their human property and protected the slave trade.
Slavery was at the heart of our republic since its beginning.
It still reverberates in our culture.
There’s nothing anti-white in pointing this out. The Founders installed in the Constitution ways to amend it, fix social problems, even change American society.
The country is an ongoing project: We’re still striving for that “more perfect union,” and acknowledging the blindingly obvious ways in which our deals don’t match up with our reality is not a heinous assault on patriotism.
CRT was developed by legal scholars, and has long been part of law school curricula. Nobody much noticed it until 2021, when a right-wing activist called Christopher Rufo kicked off a national moral panic.
You might remember Rufo from the 2024 presidential campaign, amplifying J.D. Vance’s lies about Haitians in Ohio eating cats and dogs.
Before that, Rufo had made a name for himself as a warrior against anything he saw as “woke,” especially in higher education.
DeSantis appointed Rufo to New College’s Board of Trustees (he’s since left) to help destroy what once was an admired, creative, and tolerant liberal arts school, labeling any teaching he didn’t like “Critical Race Theory.”
CRT, he said, is “the perfect villain.”
Army of lefties
Having tried to banish CRT along with sociology, the unpleasant parts of American history, the novels of Toni Morrison, and any science that might reveal things are more complicated than they’d like, DeSantis, the various mediocrities running Florida’s Department of Education, and fellow travelers such as Moms for Liberty, have convinced themselves universities are hotbeds of “Marxist indoctrination.”
Apparently, professors — especially in the Humanities and Social Sciences — are not merely “woke,” we’re a bunch of commies, determined to brainwash the Youth of Florida into hollering “Workers of the World Unite!” — assured they have nothing to lose but their chains.
Or something like that.
Alas, all my colleagues and I must be really lousy at indoctrination. I don’t know anybody who’s been successful in producing even one committed Marxist.
But DeSantis et al. are convinced higher education is a plot to produce an army of lefties.
Not that they can produce much evidence of this.
They’re more ideologically rigid than the most committed Trotskyite, and less logical than the American officer who, standing in the ruins of a Vietnamese provincial capital in 1968, told reporter Peter Arnett, “It became necessary to destroy the town to save it.”
Maybe the administration’s idea is to destroy higher ed in order to save it.
Hypotheticals
No doubt DeSantis took some comfort from the dissent in the 11th Circuit’s ruling.
Judge Barbara Lagoa, a former member of the Florida Supreme Court, (indeed, a DeSantis appointee and often mentioned as a potential U.S. Supreme Court justice), argues, what if “a professor who says that Hamas’s October 7th attack on Israel was ‘exhilarating’ and something to be celebrated and encouraged?”
She goes on to say, “Florida acts well within its authority to curb professorial endorsements of that kind within its own classrooms.”
First of all, if someone were stupid enough to say such a thing, that professor could be disciplined for creating a hostile educational environment.
But taking a hypothetical case of poor judgment and concluding somehow professorial speech must always be equivalent to the views of the state violates the First Amendment.
The First Amendment protects offensive speech — even hate speech.
In George Orwell’s essay “Freedom of the Press,” he writes, “If liberty means anything at all it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.”
Or to quote again from the majority opinion, the university’s mission is to get students to “puzzle through ideas that are good and bad, easy and hard, ideally getting ever closer to the truth.”
Professors call this “teaching.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: I’ve knocked on 4,000 doors. We need more urgency to bring down the cost of living
description: The conversations on doorsteps keep coming back to the same thing. Who will be able to live here if the cost of living keeps going up?
text:
I started knocking on doors in the February snow. Now, I’m talking to my neighbors in the boiling July heat. During my campaign for state representative in New Haven, I’ve knocked on more than 4,000 doors across Westville, Amity, Dwight, West River, Edgewood, and the Hill.  
 Across a district that is incredibly diverse, the conversations on doorsteps keep coming back to the same thing. It’s the question that has been my focus on New Haven’s Board of Alders and at Connecticut Voices for Children: Who is our state for? And who will be able to live here if the cost of living keeps going up?  

Eli Sabin

 Making New Haven and Connecticut a more affordable place to live for families, seniors, and young people has driven my work. And it’s why I think we don’t have time to wait for our state government to take on this crisis with urgency, creativity, and political courage. 
 A couple weeks ago, I talked to a woman in Edgewood who told me she was paying her rent but she was afraid she and her kids would be evicted. She asked me where she could find an affordable place to move if she lost her apartment. I’ve heard from so many seniors who are worried that their rising property tax bills are going to price them out of the homes they’ve lived in for decades. And neighbors are always bringing up our state’s out-of-control electric bills, child care costs, and the growing sense that our city and our state are just not affordable for working people and the middle class. 
 A lot of us are relieved to live in a state run by Democrats, especially as the Trump administration attacks vulnerable Americans across the country. But with the cost of living continuing to rise, we need our state government to do more. The conversations I have with voters every day highlight four changes we should take on with new energy, ideas, and strategy: 
Bring down property taxes by fixing how we fund schools. One man I talked to in Westville brought out his property tax letters to show me. He was frustrated. Over the past three years, New Haven’s tax rate has gone up 7.5 percent, and tax bills have jumped even more because of the recent property revaluation.
 Importantly, high property taxes and underfunded schools are related. About 30 percent of New Haven’s city budget goes to our schools. Our property taxes are high in part because state education funding has been largely flat since 2013. The state’s Education Cost Sharing formula has not kept up with inflation. If it had, New Haven would receive roughly $60 million more per year for our schools. That funding could help us fully staff our schools and also offset up to 7 mills of local property taxes. More state money for education would lead to better outcomes for our kids and also lower the burden on taxpayers.  
Gov. Ned Lamont recently established a commission on education funding reform. With that process underway, now is the moment for our state legislators to organize and build coalitions between rural, suburban, and urban towns. If we fight together for real education funding reform, we can make it a reality. Both taxpayers and students across Connecticut are feeling the same pinch. 
New state investment should also come with more transparency and long term financial planning from boards of education. With more resources and better accountability, we can reform our school funding system to improve our schools and lower property taxes at the same time.
Help people stay in their homes. For the woman I met facing eviction, and thousands like her, I’ll fight to pass just-cause eviction protections. Tenants who pay their rent and follow their leases should not be uprooted from their homes without a legitimate reason. Losing your home is devastating, and right now state law allows it to happen for no reason at all. That needs to change.
 Landlords have stopped this legislation from passing in recent sessions. I will work with tenant advocates and legislators from around the state to continue raising the voices of renters who need this protection. I believe that getting this legislation passed will require addressing small landlords’ legitimate concerns about rising costs and management challenges. 
We can do more to expand homeownership, too. New Haven has block after block of two- and three-family homes owned by absentee corporate landlords. Many renters would love to become homeowners, but you usually can’t buy just one unit, and buying a multifamily is too expensive. We should make it easier to convert these multi-family rentals into condos. Done right —with tenant protections to prevent displacement—this reform would give more families a real stake in our neighborhoods and a path to building wealth. 
Make daily life more affordable.  Families are also hit hard by our upside-down tax code and by high utility bills in drafty, inefficient apartments. These are two different problems that we need to address. First, Connecticut should enact a Child Tax Credit of $500 per child for families earning under $100,000 (or $200,000 for a couple), putting money in parents’ pockets to pay for the basics. The CTC should be combined with other state programs and offered as a monthly benefit that fits better with family budgets. 
 Second, tenants deserve to know what their utility bills will be before they sign a lease. I’ll push for legislation requiring landlords and utilities to partner to disclose past average utility bills when landlords advertise the rent.  
 These changes will make a real difference, but over the years, I’ve also heard something harder to fix with legislation: disillusionment. As I walk down the street, people shout out that politicians only show up for elections. Nearly every day during this campaign, someone has told me I’m the first person running for office who has ever knocked on their door or called them personally. 
 As a state representative, I’ll keep knocking on doors year-round. In this moment when people don’t believe that government can deliver, it’s more important than ever to show up and prove that we can solve the big problems we face. That starts with bold action, now, to make our state more affordable. 
Eli Sabin of New Haven is a Democratic candidate for Connecticut House District 92.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: There’s more the story on the Supreme Court decision on Roundup
description: There’s been a lot written about the safety of glyphosate, but very little concerning the   possibility that it contains an additional active ingredient.
text:
The recent Supreme Court decision concerning the labeling of Roundup pesticide (Monsanto Co. v. Darnell) has important implications.  
While lawyers discuss the legal ramifications of this decision, there is a good chance that the Supreme Court missed some very important nuances of what’s going on. There’s a debate in the scientific literature about how Roundup actually works and what exactly is/are the active ingredient(s) in the product.  There’s been a lot written about the risks of glyphosate, but very little discussion concerning an alternative possibility: that there’s an additional active ingredient or impurity in at least some batches of Roundup.
Let’s begin with a little history of a different herbicide.  Agent Orange was a defoliant developed for use in the Viet Nam war.  The idea behind Agent Orange was that by reducing the forest canopy in Viet Nam, our forces would have an easier time spotting the enemy.  
Making Agent Orange is tricky. The process needs careful temperature control to limit side reactions that produce a contaminant called TCDD (aka dioxin).  Some of the manufacturers didn’t do such a good job, and elevated levels of dioxin led to nasty diseases like chloracne and cancer.  Eventually, the Agent Orange Act of 1991 provided some relief for the injured troops.  The important take home here is that the really pernicious effects of Agent Orange were from a contaminant– not the primary ingredients.
When Roundup was being developed (patented in 1974), Monsanto, the manufacturer, told the newly formed EPA (December, 1970) that the active ingredient was glyphosate (very roughly between a third and a half of the product).  The EPA then diligently evaluated glyphosate and they probably did it correctly.  There hasn’t been a lot of advancement in evaluating such toxicity in the last several decades. 
I was in grad school in the 80s looking at how chromium(VI) causes cancer (Erin Brockavich’s claim to fame ) and if a compound doesn’t kill a mouse, well, that was a pretty good indicator that it’s probably safe for humans as well.  Glyphosate looks pretty safe to animals and humans.
Like pesticides, herbicides are often cocktails. They are frequently mixtures of active ingredients which is a similar idea as to most chemotherapy drugs and formulated for the same reason: if you want to kill something, then blocking multiple pathways is often more effective than just blocking a single pathway. These agricultural chemicals also contain formulant chemicals that are added to stabilize and solubilize the active ingredients.
There are lots of scientific papers that delve into the interaction of EPSPS, a plant enzyme, and glyphosate.  There is also a lot of literature on glyphosate which shows that its probably pretty safe to humans but can wind up where its not wanted causing environmental harm to other plants which can have ripple effects on an ecosystem.
But is that all that’s going on?  A 2019 study showed that for tomato plants, naturally water didn’t harm them, but nor did just glyphosate.  Why was glyphosate alone ineffective as an herbicide?  Probably because the added formulants have a clear purpose: they are needed to allow glyphosate to enter the plant or for some other biological activity.  There’s an additional wrinkle: when the formulants in Roundup were tested, some also showed strong herbicidal activity– without glyphosate.  What this paper suggests is that glyphosate may not be the only bio-active ingredient in Roundup.  
While the authors of this 2019 paper stated that their work was not definitive and needed additional experimentation, it certainly did open up an intriguing hypothesis: If it turns out that glyphosate is not the only bio-active ingredient in Roundup, does that help explain the numerous claims of people being injured?  There are enough claims to think that “where there’s smoke, there’s fire.”  It is pretty clear that glyphosate isn’t very toxic to humans or animals, being highly specific for plants.   But what if glyphosate is not the only active ingredient in Roundup?
The only component in pesticides that EPA tested extensively in the 1970s was the active ingredient.  Formulants are considered “inert” by the EPA and were only tested as part of the entire package of Roundup– not individually.  That’s concerning because clearly, most of the effort by the EPA was devoted to making certain the active ingredient is safe.
There’s another problem: the EPA uses an “unusual” definition of inert which is that anything that is not the active ingredient is considered inert.  Most of us think that inert simply means inactive, but some formulants in one pesticide (considered “inert”) can be listed as active ingredients in another.  This EPA definition is rather confusing. Note that the label on the pesticide doesn’t have to disclose what formulants are in the pesticide or their relative amounts because companies consider that information proprietary.  Formulants are typically present in lower concentrations than the “active” ingredients which theoretically makes them less risky.  This is not a good assumption.  That’s what led to the debacle of Agent Orange and has likely led to some people being injured by Roundup.
Some researchers think that the ingredients of Roundup have varied over the years. What would be the issues if  some scientists at Monsanto might have become concerned that one of the formulants could sometimes have potential toxic effects, and what if some of these researchers may have suggested alternatives?  This possibility certainly adds some additional complexity to this situation if correct.
In the 1990s, the situation gets even more convoluted.  Roundup wasn’t really all that popular when it was first introduced, but by the mid 1990s it was a very profitable agricultural product— especially when combined with sales of the genetically modified seeds. Yes, these seeds are one of the company’s major GMO products and accounted for more of Monsanto’s profit than Roundup itself.  Are the seeds only modified to be resistant to glyphosate?  Or are there other modifications too?
This is why the Supreme Court decision is worrisome.  While this hypothetical is not meant to explore causation or connection between the product and any injury or to imply any wrongdoing, it is worth thinking about in our world of ever-increasing cancer rates and environmentally affected illnesses. If there is even a chance that someone at Monsanto may have acted unethically or did not identify all of the all the actual active ingredients in Roundup to the EPA in any formulation during all these years would the company be entitled to get away with it at the potential expense of thousands of injured individuals?  
Isn’t that the net effect of what the Supreme Court has come up with?  Then if people did actually did get hurt, are they left with no recourse?
Samuel Brauer, the founder of Nanotech Plus, LLC, lives in Shelton.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Water main break closes West Main Road in Middletown, prompts boil water advisory
description: Approximately 2,000 customers of the city of Newport’s Water Division public water system were advised to boil water before drinking it as a precautionary measure Sunday as crews worked overnight to repair a water main break underneath West Main Road in Middletown.   A bell joint failed on a 24-inch water main on the southbound side […]
text:
Crews work on repairing a broken water main underneath West Main Road in Middletown Sunday, July 19, 2026, at around 5 p.m. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Approximately 2,000 customers of the city of Newport’s Water Division public water system were advised to boil water before drinking it as a precautionary measure Sunday as crews worked overnight to repair a water main break underneath West Main Road in Middletown. 
 A bell joint failed on a 24-inch water main on the southbound side of the the state road, Route 114, between the entrances to the shopping plaza home to Staples, The Home Depot, Aldi and other retail stores, according to a notice posted by the City of Newport Public Water System. The break caused a loss of pressure in the system, which increases the risk that untreated water or other contaminants could potentially enter the pipes. The notice includes a map of neighborhoods impacted by the boil water advisory.
The Rhode Island Department of Health issued an alert about the advisory Sunday night. Boiling kills bacteria and other organisms in the water. 
Motorists first reported asphalt buckling across the entire width of West Main Road at around 10 a.m. For the remainder of the day, the road was closed to traffic between the access road and Valley Road. Police advised motorists to avoid the area if they could. 
Repaving on the northbound side of the roadway was estimated to be completed by 4 a.m. Monday, allowing for southbound traffic to use one of the northbound lanes for the morning commute, Middletown Fire Chief Rob McCall said.
The boil water advisory will remain in effect for approximately two to three days, even after water service returns. Two rounds of water samples collected 24 hours apart must show the water is safe before the Rhode Island Department of Health can authorize lifting the order. 
The town’s fire station served as the emergency operation center for most of Sunday. Between 2 and 8 p.m., the John F. Kennedy Elementary School was a distribution point for bottled water for residents after their water service was shut off, including those living at East Bay Village and Northgate Apartments, McCall said. Bottled water was available at the fire station Sunday night.

title: Labor memorializes 92nd anniversary of ‘Bloody Friday,’ as history rhymes
description: When Minneapolis police sprayed bullets into a crowd of hundreds of strikers in 1934, John Hanson’s father plugged wounds to stop blood from seeping into the cobblestone.  “My father approached the closest fallen man, who was moaning, screaming and bleeding into the pavement,” he said. “Can you imagine what those cracks we’re looking like?” Standing […]
text:
Minneapolis-based activist band Brass Solidarity perform "When the Saints Go Marching In during the annual Remember 1934 event in the city’s warehouse district on Sunday, July 19. (Photo by Peyton Haug/Minnesota Reformer) 
When Minneapolis police sprayed bullets into a crowd of hundreds of strikers in 1934, John Hanson’s father plugged wounds to stop blood from seeping into the cobblestone. 
“My father approached the closest fallen man, who was moaning, screaming and bleeding into the pavement,” he said. “Can you imagine what those cracks we’re looking like?”
Standing 92 years later on the same ground, Hanson the younger lamented the deaths of Henry Ness and John Belor — the two union members police killed after shooting nearly 70. 
“In the end, victory took mutual aid, caring for one another, coalition building, trust, solidarity and resilience,” he said. 
Hanson’s father, also named John Hanson, was a coal truck driver and member of the Committee of 100, a group of union leaders elected to manage the 1934 strikes and union activity beyond. 
His recollection was among the stories striker descendants shared with the nearly 100 people who gathered Sunday for an annual event remembering tribulations surrounding what’s known as Bloody Friday.
The 1934 shooting was a crescendo of a months-long battle between the truckers and warehouse workers of Teamsters Local 574, and the “Citizens Alliance,” who were the corporate owners trying to suppress workers’ pursuit of fair wages and working conditions. 
Marchers memorialized Henry Ness and John Belor on Sunday in Minneapolis. Police killed the two men after shooting nearly 70 during Bloody Friday in July 1934. (Photo by Peyton Haug/Minnesota Reformer)
President Franklin Roosevelt eventually intervened to hand the workers a victory. The companies succumbed to worker demands, and union participation exploded in Minnesota and across the country. Teamsters 574’s membership alone grew from 175 to more than 5,000 workers.
History rhymes 
The solidarity theme remained center stage, but this year’s memorial was different. 
On the sweltering, smoky Sunday afternoon, history’s rhymes sang loudly through the city as crowds paused for a bit longer to remember the slain Renee Good and Alex Pretti — the two Minneapolitans shot and killed by immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge. 
They also memorialized Victor Manuel Díaz, a Nicaraguan man who died in ICE custody. 
“The organizing of rapid response, mutual aid and the many ways people came out to defend their neighbors during Operation Metro Surge, it was like the way the community was responding to the Teamsters strike in 1934,” said event organizer Peter Rachleff. 
He taught and studied American history for decades at Macalester College, focusing largely on immigration and labor.
Rachleff said there are echoes this winter of labor battles past: “It’s this idea that word would get out about a point of conflict, and a whole bunch of people would show up.” 
Among the parallels to “Bloody Friday”: The two civilian deaths; frequent tear gas deployment during street battles; creative civil disobedience tactics; and hundreds of thousands of people flooding the streets — for Ness’ funeral and the 2026 general strike. 
‘Why work if you can’t make enough to live anyway?’
Between growing up listening to his fathers stories and watching the Minneapolis labor movement evolve, Hanson said he has noticed a Great Depression-era mindset resurfacing: “Why work if you can’t make enough to live anyway?’”
“A lot of people, younger people, are coming into these industries, seeing the unfairness and wanting to do something about it,” he said, citing union drives spanning across sectors, from health care and higher education to the service industry. 
Hanson said his father would be pleased to see how labor and allied groups coalesced during Operation Metro Surge. 
The temporary political victory during Operation Metro Surge comes at a difficult time for labor unions, however: President Donald Trump ended collective bargaining for more than 1 million federal workers, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported this year that the number of wage and salary workers belonging to unions was 14.7 million in 2025, or 10%, which was down from 17.7 million and 20% in 1983, the first year for which comparable data are available. 
Sunday’s remembrance closed off with music from Brass Solidarity. The activist brass band marched the streets in a fashion reminiscent of the New Orleans second-line celebrations known for honoring the dead. 
Carpenter and musician Emmett Doyle also performed an original song called “the 1934 Strike Song.” 
He is among the Minnesota 15 who were indicted in May and are being accused of impeding the feds during their immigration operations.  
“The (Trump) administration is terrified of the power of the general strike and the power of mass resistance. They think that by targeting a small number of radicals, they can cleanse the city of a tint of leftism,” Doyle said. 
For now, local unions are focusing on the Faster Labor Contracts Act, according to Paul Slattery of Teamsters Local 120. The bipartisan bill would fast-track collective bargaining agreements between employers and newly formed unions — a common management tactic is to delay contract negotiations, hoping the new union will die on the vine.   
“Whether it’s ICE, whether it’s more labor organizing, the fight continues for workers rights, and peoples’ rights,” he said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Eight Roxbury Correctional Institution inmate stabbings over July 4 revive staffing questions
description: A July 4 weekend brawl at Roxbury Correctional Institution in which eight inmates were stabbed and hospitalized has renewed scrutiny of conditions at state prisons, with a lawmaker and labor leaders saying it points up short-staffing problems.
text:
Roxbury Correctional Institution near Hagerstown. (Photo courtesy Hagerstown Herald-Mail)A July 4 weekend brawl at Roxbury Correctional Institution in which eight inmates were stabbed and hospitalized has renewed scrutiny of conditions at state prisons, with a lawmaker and labor leaders saying it points up short-staffing problems.
“They’re mandating folks to work 16-hour shifts over and over again,” said Linda He, a spokesperson for the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Maryland Council 3, which represents Roxbury staff. “They’re losing the folks who are really experienced because they’re burned out, you know? Why do this work when the pay isn’t ever going to keep up or make the work worth it?”
Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services officials acknowledge long-term staffing problems, which they say they have been successfully working to address, but they insist that staffing issues had nothing to do with the stabbings in early July.
“We want to be clear: This incident was not the result of short staffing. Our operational assessments confirm that adequate security protocols were – and remain – in place, and that this event was unrelated to current staffing levels,” said Yianni Varonis, the department’s spokesperson.
The July stabbings come against a backdrop of rising homicides at state prisons. There have been 32 homicides investigated at state prison facilities since 2023 – more than half of all inmate killings recorded since 2015. There were two inmate killings at Roxbury in May including the death of Colin Wolf, 32, in his cell, a death that led to the departure of Roxbury’s warden and administrative charges against 19 officers.
“The violence at Roxbury is unfortunately nothing new,” He said.
A cellblock at Roxbury Correctional Institution. (Photo courtesy Hagerstown Herald-Mail)
State Sen. Paul Corderman (R-Washington and Frederick) visited the prison July 8, after his office got calls and emails about the holiday weekend violence. During that visit, he said he got to speak with new Warden Damean Stewart.
One of the biggest challenges Corderman said he has seen during his time in Annapolis, as both a delegate and senator, since 2017: staffing.
“God bless the staff there now,” he said. “But things must improve.”
After a visit that lasted more than 30 minutes, Corderman said he got a phone call from Public Safety and Correctional Services Secretary Carolyn Scruggs, and a July 10 letter from Scruggs. In the letter, Scruggs said it was “regrettable” she could not meet with Corderman on short notice, and agreed the health and safety of staff and those incarcerated is “of the highest priority,” She also outlined how she’s reduced the vacancy rate during her tenure.
The year before Scruggs was appointed in 2023 by Gov. Wes Moore (D), the vacancy rate was 15.36% but it has been cut almost in half, to 8.42%, since then, according to Varonis. He said it was a problem inherited from the previous administration.
“Between January 2015 and January 2023, 1,796 correctional positions were eliminated in the State budget, hampering the ability of the Moore Administration to adequately staff State correctional facilities,” Varonis said.
“Since 2023—in collaboration with the union, correctional experts, budget analysts, and the General Assembly—most of those lost positions have been restored,” he said.
Still, Scruggs wrote to Corderman that more work needs to be done “to shore up staffing” in Western Maryland, where Roxbury is, and in Eastern Shore facilities.
“As you know, those are the most challenging regions of the State to recruit and sustain employment while ensuring the Department is hiring correctional officers that meet the highest standards of conduct established,” Scruggs wrote. “These are issues that cannot be resolved over a 30-minute meeting with the newly appointed Warden at RCI or a 20-minute phone call with me. I invite you to partner with me and work together.”



Quotation







“I think the biggest thing, especially as far as the staff, because you're not going to be able to staff overall, is having the National Guard come in to support. It may sound, you know, as an extreme measure, but we're in an extreme situation here, and everything's got to be on the table.


– Sen. Paul Corderman (R-Washington and Frederick), on staffing issues at state correctional institutions


Staffing problems are part of a statewide and national issue, said Wanda Bertram, communications strategist for the Prison Policy Initiative, a criminal justice research and advocacy group. Without adequate staffing, correctional facilities in other states have turned to short-term solutions like lockdowns, which present safety and health issues for inmates.
But Bertram also said more hiring isn’t the only solution to the staffing problem.
“The other way to right-size these population imbalances is to let people out of prison,” she said, adding that advocates have long called for making it easier for inmates who pose the lowest risk to return to their communities.
She pointed to inmates over 55, inmates in for minor offenses and those already close to their release dates as prime examples of people whose release could alleviate the challenge faced by facility staff.
“You know, if you want to release 1,000 people from prison, you can do it. We saw that happen during COVID 19,” she said, pointing to states like California, North Carolina and New Jersey that released thousands of inmates early after the onset of the pandemic.
Broad and swift releases of inmates would require action from the governor or lawmakers, but Bertram said there are still actions that can be taken.
“Maryland is a state that has parole,” she said. There are ways to “get more hearings going,” she said, including by adding hearing examiners.
Hearing officers and examiners, which often review cases alone and make recommendations to the commissioners, are hired at the discretion of the DPSCS secretary.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“These are all ways that you can lower the size of the prison population that can allow departments to consolidate people in facilities that are better staffed,” Bertram said. “I don’t think that should be left off the table the way that it seems to.”
What’s “absolutely not” on the table for Corderman is letting inmates out of prison before their sentence is up.
“The unfortunate reality is these individuals are in prison for a reason. I have no appetite for prisoner release,” he said. “That is ludicrous. I can’t talk strongly enough against that.”
Corderman said he hopes to improve maintenance at the facilities, like air conditioning and fire alarms, and take the staffing issue seriously. For Corderman, that includes the possibility of deploying the National Guard if needed.
“I think the biggest thing, especially as far as the staff, because you’re not going to be able to staff overall, is having the National Guard come in to support,” he said. “It may sound, you know, as an extreme measure, but we’re in an extreme situation here, and everything’s got to be on the table.”
Whatever the solution, Bertram and He both said that they hope the state can get things done.
“All of us are working together to basically hold the decisionmakers accountable,” He said. “Because until there’s changes, people’s lives are going to be at risk and people’s lives are going to be lost, whether it’s incarcerated individuals or its staff.”
Corderman said the topic of public safety at correctional facilities may come up when the legislature convenes for a special session Aug. 3-5, even though the session was called specifically for redistricting efforts.
“Anytime there’s a session, we can bring all cards on the table,” he said. “We are always open for that. Definitely a possibility,” Corderman said. “Whether the [Democratic] majority wants to do something about that, we’ll see what happens.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez make electability case for El-Sayed
description: Questions of electability have loomed large for Abdul El-Sayed as he inches toward the finish line in a tight Democratic race for the U.S. Senate — both as a progressive candidate against a more establishment opponent in the August primary but also as it concerns the general election in November. A rally held in downtown […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, left, U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, center, and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, right, at a rally in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. The rally also included U.S. House candidate William Lawrence. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Questions of electability have loomed large for Abdul El-Sayed as he inches toward the finish line in a tight Democratic race for the U.S. Senate — both as a progressive candidate against a more establishment opponent in the August primary but also as it concerns the general election in November.
A rally held in downtown Lansing on Sunday, featuring U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), aimed to bolster El-Sayed’s viability in his race against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham). It also served the purpose of raising the argument that he can win in November against the presumed Republican candidate, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake. 
The progressive roadshow in Michigan included a stop in Detroit on Saturday, featuring Sanders but also U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit), UAW President Shawn Fain and 13th Congressional District candidate Donavan McKinney, who faces incumbent U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit). Following the Lansing rally, the Democratic Socialist revue traveled to Grand Rapids later Sunday as a trio with Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez and El-Sayed in tow.
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a rally with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
‘In all, both Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez, representing the old and new guard of the progressive left, told committed supporters and potential new voters that El-Sayed can win his race on Aug. 4 against the centrist U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) and would go on to win against Rogers in the fall.
For Sanders, the immediate horizon was not just a gateway to the real race in November — it was a battle for the soul of the Democratic Party in Michigan.
“There is a reason why the whole country is watching this race. In fact, people all over the world are watching what’s happening here in the state of Michigan,” Sanders said to a sold-out crowd of 1,600 people, packed into a convention hall at the Lansing Center just blocks from the state Capitol. “The reason for that is, that in a time when we have more wealth and more inequality than we have ever had in the history of this country, at a time when fewer people, a handful of people, have never held so much wealth and power in the history of this country, people all over America and the world are asking: Is democracy alive and well in America? 
“Or will a handful of billionaires and their super PACs be able to buy this election?”
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks at a rally for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. The rally also included U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
To Sanders’ point, the race has brought in all kinds of outside spending on behalf of the candidates, and much of it in favor of Stevens and against El-Sayed. AdImpact reported on July 13 that, over the next week, over-the-air TV advertising is expected to land from United Democracy Project, which supports Stevens, to the tune of $4.6 million. That is in addition to the nearly $50 million in advertising already purchased to boost Stevens and defeat El-Sayed.
While El-Sayed is slated to spend his own campaign funding to get on the air, with necessary additional advertising support from outside spending, the advertising and spending in the race has been stacked against him.
Some of that advertising has come from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, which has backed Stevens in the primary and has backed Rogers during past runs for the U.S. Senate. Both Stevens and Rogers are supporters of Israel, and Stevens this month voted against some of her Democratic colleagues in the House as they pushed to end military aid to Israel. El-Sayed has stood in solidarity with the Palestinian people and has called for ending U.S. military aid to Israel.
The dynamic of the outside spending has bolstered Sanders’ assertion that the election was coming down to “oligarchy versus democracy,” he said Sunday. Sanders added that the same outside advertising schemes tried and failed in more recent races where progressives have excelled, with the ascension of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as a guiding light for progressives seeking big wins in 2026 and beyond.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The same “big idea” and “structural change for the better” rhetoric that propelled Mamdani earlier this year is the same being used to talk about El-Sayed. Sanders laid that on thick during his third rally tour featuring El-Sayed over the course of the cycle.
“This campaign is about whether we maintain the status quo — a status quo which is failing working families in Vermont, Michigan, and all over this country,” Sanders said.
The Lansing rally also featured 7th Congressional District candidate Will Lawrence, who faces a three-way Democratic primary race against former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam. Should he win in August, he would go on to face incumbent U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett of Charlotte.
Sanders spent some of his speech propping up Lawrence as he faces some headwinds for past comments made about Black Democrats, their place in upholding the establishment and a comment that their entrenchment in Democratic politics served to “defang the white left.”
AOC calls El-Sayed the future of Michigan politics
Ocasio-Cortez, who has quickly become a power player in progressive politics, also said the issues facing the nation started well before the rise of President Donald Trump, and that it wasn’t just his election that brought on a new wave of right-wing populism predicated on anti-immigrant, anti-choice and anti-diversity rhetoric.
“We have to be willing to name the mistakes that got us here, because it wasn’t just that Donald Trump won — it’s that the Democrats lost,” she said. “The moment we are willing to admit that and name some of the causes that got us here is the moment we can start turning the ship around and making things right again. … When the stakes are so high, and when more people than ever are living so close to the bone, eventually, we have to ask ourselves: ‘Is the answer to our problems the same playbook over and over again?’”
U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez speaks at a rally for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. The rally also included U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
That also requires electing progressive candidates with a real willingness to not repeat those same mistakes, Ocasio-Cortez said — including El-Sayed.
“We can choose to reward the $50 million in dark money by voting their way. … Do you think that $50 million is for free? Do you think that $50 million is an act of charity? We know how this works,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “There’s $50 million in this race because they’re expecting a return. It’s an investment in how they make back their money, by allowing all of this stuff to continue, so that you pay more and more into their pockets. That’s what that $50 million is about. So we can choose that, or we can choose Dr. Abdul Al Sayed.”
Ocasio-Cortez said that El-Sayed represents the politics of the future, not only to win the Senate majority for Democrats, but as a way “that actually changes something.”
“Abdul had all of the opportunities before him,” she said. “He could have gotten a fancy job somewhere and ignored what was happening here at home, but instead he came home and rebuilt … health departments here in Michigan. Abdul is a man of integrity and discipline, a man of faith devoted to his family, to his beautiful daughters. He is the son of workers in this state and has stood alongside them in every fight, along every step of the way, and that is why he earns the endorsement of the UAW.”
El-Sayed and Stevens have created sharp contrasts between their campaigns following the exit of former U.S. Senate candidate Mallory McMorrow. They are still fighting to pick up her supporters, and doing so as more advertising and mailers are poised to inundate undecided voters.
Unlike Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez did not mention Lawrence.
U.S. House candidate William Lawrence speaks at a rally with U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
El-Sayed confident he can beat Rogers if elected in August
Following the rally, El-Sayed spoke to members of the media. Michigan Advance asked him about the electability argument being made on his behalf, given that much of the race will now be decided by those uncommitted to either candidate.
El-Sayed pointed undecided voters to a multi-pronged question. 
“I don’t think most people walk around asking, ‘Where do I fit on the left, right?’ I think most people are walking around thinking, ‘How am I going to afford paying rent next month?’” El-Sayed said. “‘My premium is way too expensive. What happens if I get sick? I really would like to take my kids out to a nice meal, but I don’t have the money for that.’ That’s what Michiganders are asking. This campaign is answering that question.”
El-Sayed was asked a second time during that same scrum on what makes him more electable in November over Stevens against Rogers.
“Maybe we’ve actually built a campaign of real people by real people, grassroots donors investing in grassroots organizers who knock on doors across this state.” El-Sayed said. “If you can’t make a contrast with your opponent, it’s hard to win an election. If DTE is funding both Stevens and Rogers, if Blue Cross is funding both Stevens and Rogers, if AIPAC is funding both Stevens and Rogers, what’s the contrast? Maybe, just maybe, we could win campaigns by actually talking about the problems real people have, but that’s not what’s coming out of their campaign. It’s all a distraction about me.
“If their whole thing is ‘he’s bad,’ at some point you have to ask, ‘why are you good?’ I’d like to hear that.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Shah drops out, clearing Jackson’s path to winning U.S. Senate nomination
description: Nirav Shah became the second high profile Democrat to drop out of the U.S. Senate race this weekend, all but paving the way for Troy Jackson to become the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee. Shah on Sunday also announced he was endorsing Jackson, saying, “Susan Collins, Donald Trump, and Senate Republicans are banking on disunity and […]
text:
Nirav Shah on election night (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Nirav Shah became the second high profile Democrat to drop out of the U.S. Senate race this weekend, all but paving the way for Troy Jackson to become the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee.
Shah on Sunday also announced he was endorsing Jackson, saying, “Susan Collins, Donald Trump, and Senate Republicans are banking on disunity and frustration from Maine Democrats to try and win this seat, and we are not going to give them that.”
“Maine Democrats are united, angry, and energized,” he added. “Now, that energy moves to the most important fight of all: defeating Susan Collins and flipping the United States Senate.”
Shah is the second candidate to drop out on Sunday. Secretary of State Shenna Bellows also announced the end of her bid, saying she would focus on her current role, which includes overseeing elections.
Jackson thanked Shah and Bellows on social media. 
“I appreciate your support and your endorsement,” the former Maine Senate President wrote on X in response to Shah’s announcement. “Now it’s time for all of us to come together, build the broadest possible coalition, and defeat Susan Collins. Let’s get to work.”
The three candidates also competed in the June 9 Democratic gubernatorial primaryand entered the race to replace Graham Platner after the oysterman dropped out of the U.S. Senate race amid sexual assault allegations.
Democratic county committees held conventions on Saturday and Sunday to vote on delegates to send to the state convention next week to determine who will replace Platner on the Democratic ticket. After the first day of meetings, Jackson had far more aligned delegates than anyone else running. By Sunday afternoon, he had won at least 367 of the 403 delegates that had been announced, the Bangor Daily News reported.
That included the second biggest county in the state, York, where the former Allagash logger secured 77 of the county’s 84 delegates. Jackson was endorsed by Platner and independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont, and has the backing of dozens of labor unions across the state. 
Even if delegates are aligned with one candidate, they are not required to vote for that candidate at the convention. However, with Shah and Bellows dropping out, there are few other challengers that could overcome Jackson’s support, making him the likely nominee. 
Rep. Nina Milliken (D-Blue Hill), who was the Hancock County lead for Jackson’s campaign, said she does not expect a significant number of delegates that have publicly committed to Jackson to change their minds at the July 25 convention in Bangor. 
“Regardless of whether or not there’s like a wide or small margin of error, in my mind, it would be irresponsible of us to not support Troy because that’s the clear message that was sent to us,” she told Maine Morning Star.
“The people want Troy Jackson.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: How the Democratic Party’s divide over Israel has reached Washington state
description: When the House of Representatives voted this week on a proposal to cut $3.3 billion in U.S. military assistance for Israel, the amendment failed but gathered some surprising Democratic “yes” votes.  A trio of Washington lawmakers were among those who backed the measure. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a leader in the party’s progressive wing, has been […]
text:
A protester against providing U.S. funding to Israel seen during a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol building in 2024. Divisions within the Democratic Party over U.S. support for Israel are increasingly visible in Washington state. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)When the House of Representatives voted this week on a proposal to cut $3.3 billion in U.S. military assistance for Israel, the amendment failed but gathered some surprising Democratic “yes” votes. 
A trio of Washington lawmakers were among those who backed the measure.
Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a leader in the party’s progressive wing, has been a leading critic of Israel’s war in Gaza and a consistent skeptic of providing further military aid to the country. So the Seattle-area representative’s vote for the amendment wasn’t unexpected.
But joining her was Rep. Adam Smith, who represents a neighboring district that extends south from Seattle to the north edge of Tacoma. Smith has always been a strong supporter of U.S. aid to Israel but now has two election opponents from the left. He described his vote as a message to the Israeli government.
Rep. Emily Randall, who has positioned herself on the party’s left flank, also voted for the measure. The state’s other five Democrats and two Republicans voted “no.”
The mixed vote reflects building tensions in the Democratic Party here in Washington.
While opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza has been prominent at Seattle protests over the past few years, the debate really hasn’t entered the political fray in more than a symbolic way. Until this year.
Last month, the Washington State Democratic Party approved a party platform at its convention in Spokane that mentions Israel repeatedly.
The topic wasn’t even a blip on Washington opinion polls before the 2024 presidential election, but two years later, Israel is part of the conversation.
It doesn’t appear that a candidate’s support for Israel will influence election results in Washington this fall like it likely did in New York and Colorado elections earlier this summer. Progressive advocates, candidates and electeds, who wish Israel were on the ballot, reluctantly agree. But even in races for the state Legislature, which don’t usually include talk about foreign policy, the topic is filtering in.
Embedded in the state party platform
The state Democratic Party’s 2026 platform included numerous mentions of Israel, Jews and Palestinians, including:

A statement against antisemitism that could be interpreted as saying Jewish support for Israel is partly to blame for antisemitism: “There has been a dramatic resurgence in antisemitism in recent years on all sides of the political spectrum, due in part to actions taken by the Israeli government.”
An endorsement of peace in Israel and Palestine, accompanied by a long list of ways the Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank have been mistreated without a mention of any negative treatment of Israelis. For example: “We believe Palestinians in the West Bank should be able to live with dignity and without the threat of settler violence or forced displacement from expanding Israeli settlements.” 
A statement of Palestinian rights to self-determination, but no mention of Israeli or Jewish rights in the place they also consider their homeland. 
A whole section of the document on Palestinian rights, from an end to Israeli occupation to freedom of movement and access for the Palestinian people. 

Advocate Yaz Kader says the strength of the statements in the platform reflects a growing concern, especially among younger Democrats, about U.S. dollars and weapons going to Israel to fight wars in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon.
“Elected leaders need to listen. It’s become clear that Democratic voters, even most American voters, want to stop sending weapons to Israel,” Kader said.
While polling shows American voters’ No. 1 issue continues to be the economy, including affordability and housing, Kader said the two subjects are related.
“We need to be spending our money here, not for wars abroad and certainly not for genocide,” he said.
Kader, a Palestinian who was a delegate to the party convention, said he believes only a small minority of both Democratic voters and party activists disagree with the statements in the platform.
Jewish lawmakers and members of the Democratic Party — a small minority of Washington’s population — are among those who were not pleased with what they see as the one-sided approach to the platform. Jews do not universally endorse Israel or its government, but a majority of Jews do support the existence of the Jewish state, although that support isn’t as strong among younger people.
Sen. Lisa Wellman, D-Mercer Island, was disappointed with the state party platform and believes this effort against Israel has been rising in Washington over time.
“At first, it seemed like it was very organic. And now I question that because of other information I have,” Wellman said, referring to accusations that some protests in Washington have been paid for and orchestrated by groups outside of the state.
She worries about antisemitism and, as the chair of the Senate Early Learning and K-12 Education Committee, has had constituents come to her to talk about feeling unsafe in local schools, including the University of Washington. 
Wellman said efforts to add statements to the party platform about Palestine and Israel have been going on for a few years but this is the first time, in her memory, that the efforts succeeded so well. She has seen similarly heightened efforts within the Legislature, including advocacy before the Senate Ways and Means Committee to divest from investments in any companies and products that come from Israel. 
After 10 years as a Democratic leader in the Legislature, Wellman, who is Jewish, said this year’s platform made her feel like maybe she didn’t belong in the party anymore. She said she even reached out to the chairwoman, Shasti Conrad, asking for a meeting, saying that she was thinking of leaving the party. Conrad sent a member of her team to meet with Wellman. (Conrad declined through a spokesperson to comment for this article.)
Wellman, who is not running this year and plans to retire from the Legislature in 2028, said she was not hearing from candidates that this issue is coming up during campaigning, but she is aware that some Democrats are being primaried from the left, in some cases by people who have made Israel an issue in their campaigns. 
“I don’t find, in general, in the general population that Israel is an issue at all,” she said.
Bubbling up in congressional elections
The Middle East isn’t part of the political conversation about the open seat for the 4th Congressional District in central Washington or in the only real toss-up congressional race in Washington this year, in southwest Washington’s 3rd District. Voters there appear to be making this election into a referendum on the Trump administration and how incumbent Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez has done in office.
Smith’s 9th District is a different story.
In a statement after this week’s amendment vote, the 15-term congressman who is the ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, said he was incredibly frustrated with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his government’s approach to Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon and Syria, their refusal to find partners for peace among the Palestinian people, their callous disregard for human suffering and the way the Israel government has done nothing to stop Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. 
“But after nearly two years of me raising these concerns with the Israeli government and U.S. supporters of Israel, nothing has changed. Many express sympathy for my views and assure me things will change, but that has not happened. I take this vote to try once more to get the attention of the Israeli government,” he wrote. 
Running to Smith’s left this year is Kshama Sawant, a socialist and former Seattle City Council member.
She is hearing from voters that they support many of the progressive ideas she is campaigning on, from affordable housing and rent control, to free healthcare and shutting down ICE. 
“The mass of the American working class has been to the left of the politics on offer for decades, actually,” she said. “The Israel issue is an issue in itself. It’s also representative of the overall anger.”
As Sawant sees it, “There is enormous support for ending support for Israel.”
Sawant said Americans are equally concerned about economic issues and the wars in the Middle East, and she makes a connection there. She said people see the trillion dollars being spent on the war in Iran as money that should be spent at home in the United States to support housing, education and infrastructure. 
“People are absolutely angry and fired up for change,” Sawant said.
That may be true, but whether they’ll vote differently in November remains to be seen.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Austin Ahlman suspends campaign for Nebraska’s 1st district
description: Now, the race is back between incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Flood and Democratic nominee Chris Backemeyer.
text:
Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District nonpartisan candidate Austin Ahlman in Lincoln on June 17, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN —  Austin Ahlman, a progressive journalist mounting a nonpartisan campaign for Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District, announced Sunday he was ending his run for office because of concerns over his father’s health. 
Ahlman said in a statement that his father’s cancer had returned and that he and his family had “gone from speaking about the future in terms of decades to mere months.” 
“Family comes first—always,” Ahlman said. “This decision was not easy, but the people of Nebraska deserve candidates who fight for them with 100% of their energy. I cannot do that while also giving my family the love and care they need right now.”
He announced earlier this month that he had enough signatures to be on the ballot. 
Now, the race is back between incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Flood, who handily won the district the past two elections, and Democratic nominee Chris Backemeyer . Libertarian Nik Sandman is also running. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ahlman made a splash with his campaign launch in May. Ahlman said he was running because “somebody has to stand up and do something about what’s going on in this country.” Nebraska Democrats had accused Ahlman of being a spoiler by running to split the liberal vote in the race. 
But Sunday, Democratic Party chair Jane Kleeb took a conciliatory tone and thanked Ahlman for bringing his voice to Nebraska politics.
“We know you will run and win for a seat soon. We all hope your dad gets the care he needs to heal,” Kleeb said in a statement. 
Backemeyer said in a statement Sunday that he his keeping Austin’s father and family in his prayers on social media
The 1st District comprises 12 counties, including Lancaster County, which is home to heavily Democratic Lincoln, a city whose blue voters are often overpowered by the region’s more conservative smaller cities and rural areas. 
Flood has won his past two U.S. House elections by 20 and 16 percentage points, respectively. Analysts consider the 1st District seat safely Republican, including the nonpartisan Center for Politics, The Cook Political Report and Inside Elections.
The general election is Nov 3.
