name: Florida Phoenix
title: At Leadership Blue, Pete Buttigieg says Florida Democrats can win in November
description: LAKE BUENA VISTA — A series of special and local election victories over the past year have boosted Florida Democrats’ confidence they’ll continue that winning streak into the November midterm elections. But with more than 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats in the Sunshine State, it won’t be easy. Pete Buttigieg acknowledges that reality.[...]
text:
Former Department of Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg in Lake Buena Vista on July 18, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)LAKE BUENA VISTA — A series of special and local election victories over the past year have boosted Florida Democrats’ confidence they’ll continue that winning streak into the November midterm elections.
But with more than 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats in the Sunshine State, it won’t be easy.
Pete Buttigieg acknowledges that reality.
The former Department of Transportation Secretary and 2020 presidential candidate was keynote speaker at the Florida Democratic Party’s Leadership Blue gala Saturday night at the Coronado Springs Convention Center at Walt Disney World Resort.
Ours was the 29th state he has visited since leaving the Biden administration and preparing for another potential presidential run in 2028. He acknowledged a “blue wave” could be in the offing for Democrats this fall, but emphasized that is “not automatic,” noting how congressional redistricting in red states like Florida and Texas could mitigate any gains in the U.S. House of Representatives.
“But even with that tilted playing field, I see enormous opportunity for Democrats,” Buttigieg told a group of reporters minutes after finishing his speech in front of the more than 900 people.
“I see us competing in places that would have been written off just a few months ago,” he continued. “We’re talking about states and individual districts. And we’ve seen some wins. The fact that Mar-a-Lago is now represented by a Democratic legislator right here in Florida, the fact that Miami just voted for a Democratic mayor for the first time in a generation, shows you that different things are possible. It will never be easy or automatic in more conservative areas, but it’s absolutely within reach.”
Buttigieg was referencing Eileen Higgins’ victory in the Miami mayor’s race in December, the first Democrat to win that seat in decades, and Emily Gregory‘s March win in House District 87, which had gone for Republican Mike Caruso by 19 points just a year-and-a-half before.
More stunning than that was Brian Nathan’s victory on March 24 against Republican Josie Tomkow in the state Senate District 14 seat, where he was outspent 10:1 in a district won by Republican Jay Collins by nearly 10 points in 2022.
Expectations
Buttigieg kicked off his speech by saying, “I know we can compete and win in Florida because I feel how many people here and across the country are ready for something different and ready for something better.”
Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried’s stated electoral goals sounded relatively modest — she wants to lift her party out of the superminority status it holds in both chambers of the Florida Legislature. (It would need six victories in the House and two in the Senate to get that accomplished, she said).
Other speakers during the evening included incoming Senate leader Tracie Davis, incoming House leader Christine Hunschofsky, and Orlando Democratic U.S. Rep. Maxwell Frost, fresh off being re-elected last month after no Democrat or Republican filed to challenge him before the qualifying deadline. The 29-year-old Frost brought the most energy by far of any of the speakers who took the stage at the Coronado Springs Convention Center.
Democratic U.S. Rep. Maxwell Frost speaking at the Florida Democratic Party Leadership Blue’s event in Lake Buena Vista on July 18, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix).
“Florida Democrats, let’s be honest with ourselves, many in this nation look at our state  and they don’t really see us, they see what we’re up against,” he said. “Today, many think the state’s not worth fighting for.”
The next chapter in Florida won’t be written by those “naysayers,” he continued, but by the individuals sitting in the audience. And he stressed that Democrats can’t get tripped up when labeled “socialists” or worse, such as the invective thrown their way the Republican Party of Florida’s “Sunshine Showdown” conference at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel in Hollywood last month.
“Our opposition, they’re going to call us every name in the book,” Frost said. “I don’t care if you’re a progressive, I don’t care if you’re a moderate, they’re going to call you every name in the book. Please, Florida Democrats, don’t take the bait. Every second you spend saying, ‘No, I’m not,” it’s a second you’re not talking about the issues that most Floridians care about.”
Buttigieg puts Florida Republicans on blast
Buttigieg’s appearance in Florida comes as he is prominently mentioned as a top contender for the Democratic nomination for president in 2028. Just last week, a poll by The Detroit News and WDIV-TV in Detroit of 500 voters in the battleground state of Michigan placed Buttigieg in second place, trailing only former Vice President Kamala Harris.
The former Transportation secretary touted some of his accomplishments in office while serving in the Biden administration during his 23-minute address, noting his agency had helped fund more than 70,000 infrastructure projects,  including modernizing terminals at airports in Orlando and Tampa as well as adding new truck parking spaces along the I-4 corridor.
Then he turned to Florida Republicans. He “took pleasure,” he said, in working with Republican leaders across the country to implement the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, “but not so much Republicans here in Florida,” none of whom supported that legislation.
He could always count on Florida GOP officials “to take credit for something that they voted against,” he said, specifically mentioning a press event held by U.S. Rep. Vern Buchanan with House Speaker Mike Johnson at the Sarasota Bradenton International Airport in November 2023.
As the Phoenix reported at the time, “The two men spoke in a new section under construction for the airport’s new terminal expansion project, a $100 million investment that includes a five-gate terminal, a four-lane security checkpoint and five boarding hold rooms which will seat nearly 1,000 people.”
Buttigieg noted how Gov. Ron DeSantis rejected $320 million in federal transportation funding “because the word ‘carbon’ was in the title of the program,” but later ended up taking the money. (FDOT officials called the funds “politicization of our roadways” and initially declined the money).
He laid into Florida U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the GOP’s likely nominee for governor this fall. He began by noting that Donalds “was ranked the second most far-right wing conservative in the entire U.S. House of Representatives,” referring to a 2024 “report card” by GovTrack.us.
“He tried to pass a national abortion ban, voted to overturn the 2020 election, and repeatedly voted against commonsense background gun checks for gun safety, including voting no on a safety bill that his own Florida Republicans had come to pass after the Parkland massacre,” Buttigied said. “He wants to be your governor. I think we can do better than that.”
U.S. Rep. Randy Fine of Florida’s Space Coast was another target.
“With the cost of living out of control, our nation at war, Rep. Fine committed his time in Washington to developing  unique legislation like — I’m not making this up — Protecting Puppies from Sharia Law Act.”
He then noted a November 2025 poll from Florida Atlantic University’s Business and Economic Polling Initiative reporting that nearly half of Floridians say they have considered moving out of the state due to the cost of living.
“That is not bad luck,” he said. “That is what happens when you have 27 years of one-party rule.”
When it’s proven something doesn’t work, one usually tries something else, Buttigieg said. But Republicans aren’t doing that — “They’re just trying to change the rules,” he continued, referring to the congressional redistricting that went into law in May, designed to add up to four Republican seats to the 28-member party congressional delegation.
In advance of his appearance, the Republican National Committee issued a press release blasting Buttigieg and saying all Democrats, “especially Alex Vindman, Jared Moskowitz, Darren Soto, and Kathy Castor, should be asked if they agree with their new spokesman” about a variety of alleged transgressions, specifically listing “open border and mass amnesty for illegal aliens,” “taxpayer-funded healthcare for illegal aliens,” and “Bernie Sanders-style socialist healthcare.”
The Democrats’ confab took place exactly one month before the Aug. 18 primary elections. The deadline to register to vote in that election is Monday.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Bellows drops out as Jackson takes commanding delegate lead in race to replace Platner
description: Troy Jackson is gaining momentum in the unprecedented race to replace a U.S. Senate nominee, while one of his best-known competitors has dropped out. Secretary of State Shenna Bellows announced on Sunday that she was ending her bid for the U.S Senate race to replace Graham Platner, who dropped out last week among sexual assault […]
text:
Shenna Bellows and Troy Jackson cross-endorse each other in the gubernatorial primary at a May press conference. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Troy Jackson is gaining momentum in the unprecedented race to replace a U.S. Senate nominee, while one of his best-known competitors has dropped out.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows announced on Sunday that she was ending her bid for the U.S Senate race to replace Graham Platner, who dropped out last week among sexual assault allegations.
Her announcement came ahead of the second day that county parties were meeting to elect delegates to select the new nominee. Jackson, who Bellows had cross endorsed in last month’s Democratic gubernatorial primary, leads the crowded field with far more aligned delegates than anyone else running. 
“Donald Trump’s attacks on our democracy are only accelerating, and the best way that I can serve our state and country at this moment is by focusing exclusively on my role as Secretary of State,” Bellows said on Sunday as she announced ending her candidacy.
On Saturday night, she said on social media, “no one in Maine has a track record like mine of standing up to Trump,” which is the same message she ran on in the gubernatorial primary. 
Democratic Maine Rep. Nina Milliken from Blue Hill, who was the Hancock County lead for Jackson’s campaign, told Maine Morning Star that Bellows “is the best Secretary of State Maine’s ever had, and I’m so happy she’s going to be doing that role as we go into the most dangerous election cycle this country’s ever experienced.”
But she also added that she hoped Bellows and former Maine public health chief Nirav Shah, who is also running to replace Platner, will show up at the July 25 state party convention  in Bangor and “spend their five minutes to just say, ‘Maine has spoken, and we are going to do everything we can to make sure that Troy Jackson beats Susan Collins in November.’”
Bellows has not said yet whether she will support Jackson in the U.S. Senate race. Shah’s campaign also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Jackson’s lead among aligned delegates going into the second day of county meetings is considerable. On Saturday, Democrats in eight of Maine’s 16 counties met to choose their delegates for the state convention, and Jackson jumped ahead of his competitors with what appears to be a clean sweep of delegates in several counties, according to a Maine Morning Star analysis. In Cumberland County, 149 names on Jackson’s slate of delegates matched the county’s chosen delegate list released Saturday.  His campaign also announced that every delegate chosen in Kennebec and Penobscot counties, 22 of 23 delegates in Hancock County, and 29 of 31 delegates in Androscoggin County were aligned with him. 
That means Jackson has 284 delegates named on his slate of the 500 heading to next weekend’s convention.
“I’m not surprised he’s in the lead. I’m a little surprised by the almost completely unanimous agreement statewide so far that he should be the candidate,” Milliken said. “I think that people voted for a policy position and a policy platform that Troy embodies and that Graham Platner had, and that’s why.”
Jackson was endorsed by Platner and independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont, and has the backing of dozens of labor unions across the state. However, even if delegates are aligned with one candidate, they are not required to vote for that candidate at the convention. 
York County Democrats warned of the overlap of delegate lists, where some names are listed as aligned with more than one candidate. That speaks to the rushed timeline the Maine Democratic Party is operating on, Milliken said. She also found out on Saturday that she was on both Shah and Jackson’s slate of delegates.
“How this whole process was going to pan out was built very quickly, and there was a lot of infrastructure for these campaigns that had to be built very quickly, and that’s obviously going to lead to some confusion,” she said.
“I never spoke with anyone from the Shah campaign. I have no idea how I ended up on that slate.”
Her name has since been removed from Shah’s Hancock County delegate list.

title: Board of Pharmacy sanctions licensees for criminal convictions, dispensing errors
description: A former eastern Iowa pharmacist has been sanctioned by state regulators for a 2022 conviction for sexual exploitation of a minor. Court records indicate that in 2021, Scott County deputies were granted a search warrant for the email account and cellphone of pharmacist Scott Decker of Blue Grass. The warrant was granted after police determined […]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)A former eastern Iowa pharmacist has been sanctioned by state regulators for a 2022 conviction for sexual exploitation of a minor.
Court records indicate that in 2021, Scott County deputies were granted a search warrant for the email account and cellphone of pharmacist Scott Decker of Blue Grass. The warrant was granted after police determined an email address associated with Decker was connected to the uploading of 18 photographic images that allegedly constituted child pornography. Decker was then charged with two counts of felony sexual exploitation of a minor.
In return for his promise to suspend his practice while those charges were pending, the board agreed not to pursue formal disciplinary action against Decker until the case was resolved.
In November 2022, Decker was found guilty of two counts of sexual exploitation of a minor and was sentenced to two concurrent prison terms of five years each. In February 2023, the Board of Pharmacy says, it discovered that Decker had been found guilty on the criminal charges and had been incarcerated.
More than three years later, in May 2026, the board charged Decker with knowingly making misleading or fraudulent representations in the practice of pharmacy or engaging in unethical conduct, and with being convicted of an offense that directly relates to the duties and responsibilities of the profession.
According to the board, Decker has been released from prison. He and the board recently agreed to settle the disciplinary case with Decker voluntarily surrendering his license to practice in Iowa.
Other licensees recently sanctioned by the board include:
Miola Gossman, a pharmacy technician from Decorah, who agreed to surrender her license. The board had recently charged Gossman with violating the terms of an agreement with the Iowa Professional Health Committee by failing to comply with treatment program requirements.
According to the board, that agreement was signed in January 2024 due to Gossman accruing five drunken-driving convictions between January 2022 and October 2023. Gossman also missed 50 separate check-ins with the program over a seven-month period, the board alleged.
Hy-Vee Pharmacy, which has been charged with dispensing the incorrect medication to a customer. The pharmacy in question is identified by the board only as “store no. 1136” in Des Moines. Federal records indicate that particular store is located at 3330 Martin Luther King, Jr. Parkway, Des Moines.
According to the board, the pharmacy had two patients with the same name and similar birthdates, and both patients had two prescriptions ready for dispensing on Sept. 8, 2025. The daughter of one of the patients went to pick up her mother’s medication but was sold the drugs for the other patient with the same name. The daughter alleged this same type of error had occurred previously, according to the board. The pharmacy was also alleged to have failed to complete the required reports for the September 2025 incident.
The board charged the pharmacy with negligence in the practice of the profession; divulging or revealing patient information to unauthorized individuals; and with committing medication errors resulting in the incorrect dispensing of a prescribed drug.
To resolve the case, Hy-Vee and the pharmacy board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for $3,000 civil penalty.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State leaders mourn loss of ‘greatest philanthropist in South Dakota history’
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden said this weekend that the state “will forever be impacted” by the legacy of businessman and philanthropist T. Denny Sanford. Rhoden issued his comments after First Premier Bank, Premier Bankcard and Sanford Health announced on Saturday that Sanford, age 90, had died. He owned the two companies and became the namesake […]
text:
Billionaire philanthropist T. Denny Sanford died July 18, 2026, at age 90. (Photo courtesy of First Premier Bank, Premier Bankcard and Sanford Health)South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden said this weekend that the state “will forever be impacted” by the legacy of businessman and philanthropist T. Denny Sanford.
Rhoden issued his comments after First Premier Bank, Premier Bankcard and Sanford Health announced on Saturday that Sanford, age 90, had died. He owned the two companies and became the namesake of Sanford Health — formerly called Sioux Valley — in 2007 when he donated $400 million to the organization.
Sanford’s total philanthropic contributions to numerous organizations in South Dakota and elsewhere totaled more than $4 billion.


More about T. Denny Sanford

Deal to move pork plant from downtown to northern Sioux Falls includes $50 million Sanford gift
$300 million Sanford gift ranks as fifth biggest charitable donation of the year
Full archive



“It is with great sadness that Sandy and I mourn the loss of T. Denny – a man who has so generously and intentionally invested in the great state of South Dakota,” Rhoden said in a news release. “His contributions will not be forgotten, and South Dakota will forever be impacted by his legacy. Put simply, he was the greatest philanthropist in South Dakota history.”
Sanford’s major donations in South Dakota included support for the Sanford Underground Laboratory at the former Homestake Mine in Lead, the Build Dakota and Premier/Freedom scholarships, the Sioux Falls Development Foundation’s future redevelopment of the downtown Smithfield pork plant site, Children’s Home Society of South Dakota, and Crazy Horse Memorial, among others.
“Denny Sanford was a significant donor to practically every charitable campaign in Sioux Falls, and many others throughout the state,” said Lt. Governor Tony Venhuizen. “Beyond his high-profile gifts, Denny was a key reason that Sioux Falls has such a strong culture of philanthropy, and many important community improvements benefited from his support.”
Sanford was born Dec. 23, 1935, in St. Paul, Minnesota. He lost his mother to breast cancer when he was 4, and he began working at his father’s garment shop at the age of 8. After graduating from the University of Minnesota in 1958 with a degree in psychology, he began a career in sales, marketing and materials distribution. His experiences led him to establish Contech Inc., a Minneapolis-based company that manufactured sealants, coatings and adhesives.
After selling the company, he purchased a bank in Sioux Falls in 1986. He renamed it First Premier Bank and expanded into the credit card sector with Premier Bankcard. The success of those businesses made Sanford a billionaire and allowed him to focus on philanthropy.



Quotation







His contributions will not be forgotten, and South Dakota will forever be impacted by his legacy. Put simply, he was the greatest philanthropist in South Dakota history.


– South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden on T. Denny Sanford


First Premier Bank, Premier Bankcard and Sanford Health issued joint statements on Sanford’s death. Dana Dykhouse, CEO of First Premier Bank, said Sanford told him “many people live a life of success, but you should try to live a life of significance where you can make an impact on people.” Miles Beacom, CEO of Premier Bankcard, said Sanford “could have done many things with his money, yet he reinvested it in South Dakota.”
“Our universities are stronger today because of Denny,” Beacom said. “Our health care is stronger today because of Denny. He believed in working harder to help someone other than yourself.”
Bill Gassen, president and CEO of Sanford Health, described Sanford as a “driving force in modern medicine, empowering researchers and clinicians to think big and pursue bold, innovative endeavors at a pace not otherwise possible.”
“We are able to provide care for more patients in their time of need because of his generosity,” Gassen said.
Sanford, who was twice divorced, is survived by his sons Scott and Bill, their wives, three grandchildren, and a brother, Charles “Chuck” Sanford and his wife.
Arrangements for a family service followed by a community celebration are pending.

title: ‘If we don’t write it down, it disappears’: Independent historian gathers Vermont veterans’ stories before they are lost to history
description:
What he’s trying to save isn’t just military history. It’s a way of understanding the past through another's lived experience.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘If we don’t write it down, it disappears’: Independent historian gathers Vermont veterans’ stories before they are lost to history.
text:
Soldiers salute as buglers play “Taps” at the end of a Veterans Day commemoration in Barre on Thursday, November 11, 2021. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Danielle M. Crosier was first published in the Bennington Banner on July 15, 2026.
DORSET — Charles “Max” Fish doesn’t think of history as something that lives only in textbooks or timelines. For him, it lives in the voices and the stories of everyday people — the way that someone pauses before naming a place, or the way a memory changes with perspective, maturity, knowledge and time, and with the telling.
Over the last year, the Dorset-based independent historian has been collecting those voices from Vermont veterans, recording their experiences for the Library of Congress Veterans History Project. Over the past year, his work has taken him across Southern Vermont — from American Legion halls to farm kitchens — sitting with men who went to war and then came home to towns that had mostly moved on.
What Fish is trying to save isn’t just military history. It’s a way of understanding the past through another’s lived experience, and he worries that that particular form of history is quietly disappearing from the record.
“If we don’t write it down, it disappears,” he said. “A lot of these stories only exist in one person’s memory. Once they’re gone, we’ve lost a whole way of seeing who we were.”
A life of listening
Fish’s commitment to storytelling began long before this particular and current project. As a high school sophomore, he called historical societies and a VA hospital until he found a World War II veteran willing to talk — an Army aviator named Thomas O’Rourke, who had served in the Pacific.
The resulting hourlong interview, cut to 45 minutes and paired with wartime images, became a school project. Sadly, O’Rourke died less than two years later.
“I realized that what I had from him, especially because it was so short before he died, was something really valuable,” Fish said. “It was a piece of history that wouldn’t have existed otherwise.”
Later, as a history major at Tulane University, Fish worked with a New Orleans queer archive, digitizing photographs, letters and ephemera from LGBTQ+ communities whose lives often went undocumented. “It was community preserved through history,” he said. “People who might feel isolated could see that people like them had always been there.”
Those experiences have shaped how he now thinks about archives: not as neutral repositories, but as living records that can either include or erase whole groups of people, depending on who gets asked and who gets heard.
Turning toward Vermont’s veterans
Fish discovered the Veterans History Project through National Public Radio’s StoryCorps, listening with his parents in the car. Founded in 2000, the project gathers oral histories, letters, photographs and other materials from U.S. veterans and their families.
When he moved back to Vermont and wanted to return to historical work after a stretch in retail, Fish saw an opening.
He contacted the Dorset Historical Society, where he had previously volunteered as a docent and digitized archivist, and began working independently to contribute Vermont veteran interviews to the Library of Congress collection.
Over the following roughly six to seven months — late summer and fall of 2025 into 2026 — he drove around southern and central Vermont, reaching out to historical societies and American Legion posts and asking, in essence, the same question, “Would you be willing to tell me your story?”
“At first, it was just handshakes at Legion dinners,” he said. “Once one person agreed, they’d say, ‘You should talk to my buddy,’ and it grew from there.”
Now, those interviews span Korean War service, Vietnam tours on the ground and at sea, and peacetime Cold War deployments. And, according to Fish, some of the men have never described their experiences in such detail, even to their families.
What gets lost when a story isn’t told
Fish is quick to say he’s not interested in definitive conclusions. For him, the power is in particularity — the concrete detail that never makes it into formal histories.
He talks about a submariner, Buzz Fisher, who earned his “dolphins,” the qualification pin for submariners, by learning every system on his boat. “He knew every inch of that submarine,” Fish said. “That pride, that sense of mastery — it’s a part of history you can’t see in a list of ship deployments.”
Another interview subject, Dorset’s Dave Yandell, who served on the aircraft carrier USS Ranger during Vietnam, told Fish that no one had ever simply asked him to tell his story from his own perspective, “(For him,) everyone wanted something very specific confirmed or debunked,” Fish said. “No one said, ‘What did it feel like? What did it mean to you?’”
When Fish did, Yandell described seeing the USS Ranger for the first time and then the last, tearing up and overcome with emotion at the retelling. It is those moments, Fish argues, that complicate the flat, heroic or purely critical versions of military history that can often dominate public debates.
“Official records can tell you where a unit was and when,” he said, referencing the young men who worshiped the veterans of World War II and Korea only to find themselves ostracized following service in Vietnam. “They can’t tell you what it did to someone to come home and feel like they couldn’t talk about it for 50 years.”
He worries that, without sustained efforts to collect such stories, a whole layer of historical understanding will vanish — not just facts about battles, but how those battles reshaped the people who fought them, and the communities and families that they returned to.
Barriers to an accurate historical record
Despite the importance of these accounts, Fish has found that getting them formally archived is not a simple undertaking. It is complicated. It is messy. And the subjects are often deeply unwilling.
The Veterans History Project requires veterans to sign consent forms that transfer ownership of their recorded interviews and of any donated materials to the Library of Congress. For some Vermonters, that step has been too difficult.
“Some of the men were comfortable talking to me, but not comfortable signing a document that said their story now belongs to a federal institution,” Fish said. “They’d already given up a lot of control once in their lives.”
Others hesitate for different reasons
Several Vietnam veterans whom Fish spoke with wrestle with guilt and unresolved questions about their own survival and their service — feelings that they may be willing to voice in conversation, but not ready to see published with their names forever attached.
Fish described a conscientious objector who served as a medic in Vietnam, risking his life repeatedly without carrying a weapon. In one ambush, pressured by the chaos around him, he set aside his medical kit to haul ammunition for a machine gunner — an act that technically violated the terms of his conscientious objector status.
“Everyone in his unit saw what happened and understood why,” Fish said. “But from his perspective, putting that on the record is complicated. It’s not just about policy, it’s about how he sees himself.”
Additionally, there are even more deeply rooted concerns about reprisals and judgments that could come in the wake of exposure — and fear of appearing critical or disloyal to those who served alongside them, to the chain of command under which they served, to the mission that they believed themselves to be fighting for, or to the decision-makers in the federal government. It’s almost like a collective case of Stockholm syndrome.
“You hear, you know, like ‘no man left behind,’ but that’s only true when you can afford it to be. And, I think what I hope people take away is that men like (those interviewed) are just average everyday Americans in impossible situations. You hear about stories like ‘Hacksaw Ridge’ and ‘Saving Private Ryan’ and you think, ‘That’s got to be Hollywood’ until you meet men that have actually walked and lived those stories,” Fish said. “I hope that … it just becomes a little more real to people.”
“And again, we as Americans have been so disconnected from war for so long (even though) our Army’s been fighting in every single war all over the place, but not (on the home front)”, Fish said.
A loyalty that can often complicate the truth of a lived experience
One of the most striking patterns in Fish’s interviews is the tension that he has found veterans feel between loyalty to the military and honesty about the feelings of what they lived through.
Around the stories of battles and bases, he hears a quieter struggle — a struggle of men who still love the institution that shaped them, yet carry deep doubts about the wars that they were sent to fight.
Every veteran he spoke with remembered training with true and deep affection — the sense of purpose, the discipline, the friendships that formed under pressure.
“Whether you come in because you’ve got nothing better to do, or because you’ve always wanted to be there, you come out part of something bigger than yourself,” Fish said. “Every single person I talked to really values that feeling.”
But he also found a sharp divide between those who served at a distance and those who were face to face with combat. Sailors on aircraft carriers recalled celebrating after dropping their “millionth ton” of TNT. Infantrymen in the jungle, by contrast, emerged with what Fish describes as a kind of permanent disillusionment.
“The men who were right on the front lines often had a very different takeaway,” he said. “They realized that all of the lies that had been told to them up until that point were just that: lies. It becomes this desperate, chaotic scramble to survive.”
Many of those front-line veterans, especially from Vietnam, told Fish privately that they felt the war should never have been fought, or that it was abandoned in a way that betrayed both allies and the American dead.
Yet, despite their convictions, when it came time to sign the Library of Congress paperwork, they pulled back. They worried that speaking plainly would “do a disservice to the institution,” as one man put it, or undermine the pride and identity that service had given them and given to others, including those who serve today.
In short, it was a brotherhood, and one that they could not betray. And, for Fish, that reluctance is itself a crucial part of the story.
“These are men who still feel bound to the people they served with and to the uniform they wore,” he said. “They’re proud of the training and the camaraderie, even as they question the reasons they were sent. That makes it incredibly hard to put their full truth on the permanent record – but it’s exactly why those stories matter.”
Stories as a safeguard and on the record
Fish has completed and submitted several interviews to the Library of Congress, with more in the editing queue as he prepares to leave for Austria to pursue graduate study. But he’s also keenly aware that many of the stories he’s heard will likely remain off the official books, preserved only in his notes and in his memory.
“Even when the paperwork doesn’t get signed, the conversations still matter,” he said. “They’re a reminder of how much history never makes it into the archive at all.”
Underneath the practical information about the Veterans History Project and how people can participate is a quieter argument: that listening to individual stories is not a sentimental exercise but a form of civic responsibility.
“We’re in a country where most of us are several steps removed from war,” he said. “If we only understand it through movies, speeches, textbooks or policy debates, we’re missing something essential.”
Fish believes that hearing veterans describe, in their own words, what they saw and how it changed them offers a check against abstraction — the kind that can make it easier to accept future conflicts without fully grasping their human cost.
At the same time, he resists framing veterans solely as symbols or lessons. “These are ordinary people in impossible situations,” he said. “Their stories are a part of our history, whether we record them or not. The question is whether we’re willing to listen in time.”

title: Trump sics his wretched Department of Homeland Security on Nevada’s free and fair election
description: “We refute these claims,” Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said Friday in response to the latest baseless allegations and crude extortion threats hurled at Nevada and its elections from Trump and his lap dogs. Aguilar found himself issuing more than one statement about Trump’s attacks on Nevada elections as the past week came to […]
text:
Trump has repeatedly said he wants to "take over the voting." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has indicated he's down with that. (DHS photo by Tia Dufour)
“We refute these claims,” Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said Friday in response to the latest baseless allegations and crude extortion threats hurled at Nevada and its elections from Trump and his lap dogs.


Aguilar found himself issuing more than one statement about Trump’s attacks on Nevada elections as the past week came to a close. The one quoted above was responding to snarling and barking at Nevada by Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. 
Mullin’s growling Friday came on the heels of Trump’s speech Thursday night, in which Trump reiterated for the eleventy-billionth time some of his favorite conspiracies — teeming hordes of noncitizens, all of them transgender of course, voting in elections, that sort of thing. (And yes, I may be mashing up some of Trump’s greatest hits there.) 
“That was some bullshit,” Aguilar, in his capacity as chair of the Democratic Association of Secretaries of State, said about Trump’s speech.
Aggressively ignoring that under the Constitution states, not Trump and let alone Mullin, are in charge of running their own elections, Mullin Friday dog-paddled in Trump’s wake and said states better do as Trump says or they’ll lose federal money, and state election officials might even be prosecuted.


The day before, Mullin had sent whiny letters to a few secretary of state offices around the country.


In the Nevada version of the letter, Mullin said a “preliminary review” indicated nearly 16,000 “noncitizens” are registered to vote in the state.


Aguilar dismissed that preposterous allegation as “wildly speculative at best” and accurately noted Mullin “hasn’t shared anything that backs it up.”


“The Administration lacks a fundamental understanding of how elections work,” Aguilar added.


The Trump administration lacking a fundamental understanding of things is generally a safe bet. (See Hormuz, Strait of.)


And Trump, Mullin, and the rest of the people in Trump’s administration who believe Trump’s election conspiracies and lies (or are pretending to believe them because it’s a job requirement) routinely demonstrate that any concern for elections functioning fairly and properly is the last thing on their minds.


Aguilar hinted at that a couple times near the end of the week. He described Trump’s warmed-over pig slop of a speech Thursday night as “the latest chapter in a predictable playbook crafted intentionally to undermine faith in our elections.” And in his response to Mullin’s remarks Friday, Aguilar observed that Trump and his apparatchiks “just want to cause chaos and doubt ahead of the midterms.”


“Attempts to spread misinformation and create distrust make people question a process that works and threaten to stop them from participating and voting,” Aguilar said.


Yup. That’s our Trump.


Undermining public faith in democracy so people won’t vote and/or won’t trust election results is despicably loathsome and anti-American. And yet even that, which Trump has been doing for years, doesn’t match the intensity of Trump’s second-term radicalization or the callous and blatant disregard he’s showing for everyone and everything everywhere except himself. 
In other words, it seems unlikely Trump is merely content with undermining public faith in democracy.


Trump has repeatedly said he wants to “take over the voting.”


For him to attempt do that, perhaps by deploying ICE or other, more competent armed federal forces, still might seem unthinkable. But then, so did launching a war against Iran and losing it.


As you may have heard, some Nevadans have chosen to believe Republican governor and self-styled Trump-whisperer Joe Lombardo will save us; that the governor’s staggering charm and mad skills of persuasion would combine with his purportedly Western lawman-style sense of uprightness and decency (“I’m Joe Lombardo”) to prevent Trump from, say, deploying shock troops to forcibly seize control of ballots, polling places, tallying procedures, and the election (even though as a consequence of such a takeover Lombardo’s reelection would be assured).


Yet the founding assumption underlying the “Lombardo will save us” proposition is that Lombardo’s influence with Trump is protecting Nevadans — including presumably its all-important tourism industry — from despicable actions by Trump’s immigration enforcement thugs.


Too bad the Lombardo-Trump accord, if in fact there is one, was evidently unbeknownst to the blundering ICE thugs who made international headlines with an ugly botched attempt to arrest a 57-year-old man at Harry Reid airport, suggesting to people the world over in the process that flying into Las Vegas is a dangerous proposition.


Lombardo didn’t thwart the ICE thugs at the airport. People did. And people, specifically Nevada voters, are the ones who ultimately will have to defeat Trump’s perpetual malevolent assaults on democracy in Nevada.

title: Vermont’s new education law pays districts to merge. It doesn’t make them save.
description:
Act 170 sets deadlines and creates regional service areas but leaves out efficiency targets, oversight and any requirement that savings actually materialize before construction aid flows.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s new education law pays districts to merge. It doesn’t make them save..
text:
This commentary is by Sriram Srinivasan, a retired business executive whose analysis of Chittenden County school district consolidation has been submitted as written testimony to the Vermont Senate Committee on Education.
Vermont’s education transformation bill, H.955, is now law. Gov. Phil Scott signed it on June 18, telling districts to “hit the ground running.” They certainly need to: Under what is now Act 170, districts have until Sept. 15, 2026, to assign a board member to their merger study committee; those committees begin work Oct. 15, 2026; seven cooperative educational service areas formed July 1, 2026, and the foundation formula arrives in 2029. But between signing and execution lies a gap nobody has named: no efficiency target, no oversight body, no clear picture of what success looks like when all the committee work is done.
Vermont has been here before. Act 46 merged school districts, and then watched as salary level-ups and contract renegotiations wiped out much of the projected administrative savings. The savings disappeared not because the concept was wrong, but because nobody built accountability into the execution plan. Act 170 is a better-designed law, but the same risk is present, and there is less time to address it than it might appear.
Four structural gaps deserve immediate attention from CESA boards, legislators and the districts now assigning members to merger study committees.
Act 170 creates two parallel structures: CESAs for shared back-office services, and merger study committees to evaluate voluntary district consolidation. The assumption is that these reinforce each other — that districts building shared services will develop the trust needed to consider mergers. 
That assumption breaks down when CESA members and merger committee members don’t align. CESA boundaries were drawn through one political negotiation and merger group assignments through another, leaving districts in several regions asked to build shared infrastructure with one set of partners while evaluating their futures with a different set. As of Sept. 15, 2026, districts must navigate that tension without any guidance on how to reconcile it.
The Joint Fiscal Office’s own fiscal note on June 18 states that potential CESA savings are unclear due to “outstanding service unknowns including their range, cost, and participation.” That is accurate as a statement about the law. It does not have to be true region by region. 
Based on my own analysis of Agency of Education publicly available staffing data, there is $9 million to $10 million in back-office savings available to the six Chittenden Central CESA districts alone — information technology, facilities, transportation, finance and human resources — with no impact on programming and no mergers required. But Act 170 contains no requirement that any CESA pursue savings like these, no baseline to measure progress and no accountability mechanism if they don’t. A CESA board can satisfy the letter of the law and never capture a dollar of the efficiency that justified creating the structure. That is not a framework for transformation. It is a framework for compliance.
Act 170’s most concrete incentive for mergers is financial: Merged districts receive up to 75% state construction aid versus 30% for those that don’t consolidate. But the law does not require merged districts to demonstrate operational savings before accessing that aid. A district can consolidate, claim the full package and still operate duplicated finance departments, IT systems and facilities teams underneath the merged governance structure. The merger earns the incentive. The savings are optional. Construction aid conditioned on merger is a policy choice. Construction aid conditioned on merger and demonstrated savings is fiscal stewardship. The Legislature still has the 2027 session to attach it before the first merger committees report back.
The foundation formula arrives in 2029 irrespective of whether CESAs have delivered savings. Districts that capture back-office efficiencies will enter that transition with a fiscal cushion. Those that treat CESA membership as a compliance exercise will face it without one.
Vermont’s Agency of Education has no defined role in the implementation of Act 170. Education remains the only functional area of Vermont state government without a dedicated legislative oversight committee. The closest thing to a shepherd for this process is the superintendent’s association — a valuable professional network, but not an accountability body. 
This is not an argument for top-down control. Local communities should own this work, and best results will come from within each region. But local ownership and statewide accountability are not opposites. New York’s system of boards of cooperative educational services succeeded by giving local entities both autonomy and a clear destination. Vermont has given its CESAs the former. The latter is still missing.

READ MORE

The Legislature has an opportunity in its next session to require what the law does not yet contain: defined efficiency targets for each CESA, a state-level oversight body with reporting obligations, and baseline operational data before construction aid flows to merged districts.
The savings are there. The model works. The clock, starting Sept. 15, 2026, and running to 2029, is no longer abstract. Vermont should not arrive at 2029 with emptied construction aid coffers, frustrated merger committees and the same per-pupil costs it started with.

title: At Vermont’s Estey Organ Museum, many donations total $10. Then came one so big, it paid off the mortgage.
description:
“It’s an amazing surprise,” a volunteer at the Brattleboro landmark — once home to the world’s largest manufacturer of pump and pipe instruments — says of a recent five-figure gift from another local nonprofit.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  At Vermont’s Estey Organ Museum, many donations total $10. Then came one so big, it paid off the mortgage..
text:
Visitors can play the instruments at Brattleboro’s Estey Organ Museum, located at the former home of the world’s largest manufacturer of pump and pipe models. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger
BRATTLEBORO — Volunteers at this town’s Estey Organ Museum are used to a symphony of sounds at the former home of the world’s largest manufacturer of pump and pipe instruments.
“In its heyday, the Estey Organ Company factory was the beating, bleating heart of Brattleboro,” the online travel guide Atlas Obscura begins its review of the current attraction.
But everybody went silent when peers at the local historical society, having recently banked several general bequests, arrived to announce they wanted to pay off the museum’s mortgage.
“It’s an amazing surprise,” museum board president George Wiese said of the $35,000 gift, which represents the remaining half of a loan taken out two decades ago. “I’ve spent my career in nonprofit leadership, and I’ve never seen this happen.”
The windfall comes nearly a quarter century after the society helped found the museum — located in one of seven Birge Street factory buildings that now house other businesses — to quench continuing curiosity about a local company that sold a half-million organs worldwide from 1852 to 1960, including one to automaker Henry Ford, who rolled into Brattleboro in 1915 to see a model specially crafted for his Michigan mansion.
“We know how hard it is to run an organization with little money,” Lee Ha, leader of the historical society, said of its motivation to use bequests from the local Kirkland and Philbrick families to cover the mortgage.
The donation offers new opportunities for a museum that tells Estey’s Charles Dickens-meets-Horatio Alger story without its own paid staff, just help from $10 suggested admission and $30 annual memberships.
“The word that comes to my mind is ‘transformative,’” Wiese summed up the gift, which will allow $6,000 in past annual mortgage payments — almost 40% of the operating budget — to go toward preserving more instruments.
Brattleboro often traces its history back to the 1724 founding of Fort Dummer, the first permanent European settlement in what’s now Vermont. But the town didn’t find itself on the map until the late New Englander Jacob Estey, born into poverty in 1814, ran away as a child laborer at age 13 and worked a series of odd jobs before establishing his namesake company a decade before the Civil War.
The Estey Organ Co. catered to customers seeking entertainment in the era before electronics. 
“Estey’s flagship product was the reed organ, a musical chimera with the air power of an accordion, the metal reeds of a harmonica, and the keys of a piano,” Atlas Obscura summarizes for visitors today. “Cheaper than pianos and easier to maintain, they became a staple of the middle-class family parlor.”
Estey workers manufactured 200,000 pump organs before their leader’s death in 1890, then expanded to make larger pipe instruments for such places as Hollywood’s United Artists studio.

The Estey Organ Museum on Brattleboro’s Birge Street showcases a company that sold a half-million instruments worldwide from 1852 to 1960. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Visit the museum today and you’ll learn how the company tapped such advances as the steam engine and telegraph to ship a half-million organs to homes, churches and public buildings on every continent except Antarctica.
“From the far-off pines of Siberia to the golden shores of the Pacific,” its publicity promised.
Levi Fuller, an Estey machinist and mechanical engineer, would become the company’s vice president and, from 1892 to 1894, governor of Vermont. Fellow Estey leaders made their own history, bucking tradition by paying men and women the same wage and underwriting a building at North Carolina’s Shaw University that was the first in the nation dedicated to higher education for Black women.
Estey workers stayed busy during World War II, crafting portable organs used by U.S. Army chaplains. But soon after finishing its biggest project (a $65,000 commission for Florida Agricultural and Mechanical University in 1952), the business was sold to a New Jersey firm in 1953. It closed amid the ascent of television in 1960.
“Local folklore has it that Estey employees wept while hearing a recital on the last pipe organ to leave,” Dennis Waring writes in his 2002 book, “Manufacturing the Muse: Estey Organs & Consumer Culture in Victorian America.”
When locals established the Brattleboro Historical Society in 1982, they discovered the company was gone but not forgotten. Members estimate they’ve answered more than 1,000 questions from organ owners over the past four decades, leading them to help launch the museum 20 years ago.
The exhibit hall, located in an old first-floor engine room, includes two dozen instruments on display and another 50 in storage. The space — open Saturdays and Sundays from 2 to 4 p.m. from May through October — also features a guest book with visitor signatures from two dozen states this summer alone.
Take Peter Krasinski, a Massachusetts musician and silent movie accompanist who tried several instruments one recent weekend on his way to one of his local performances.
“This is very unusual, as it’s not every place where people can play,” Krasinski said as he touched the two-tiered keyboard of a 1915 pipe organ adapted so people can see its inner workings.
The museum recently partnered with the national Organ Historical Society to place more than 150 boxes of the company’s records online. With the mortgage paid off, its two dozen volunteers are turning their attention to restoration and maintenance of models that continue to roll in, even with the oft-repeated notice, “space limitations prevent us from accepting donations of instruments that duplicate those in our collection.”
“Now every dollar,” Wiese said of the windfall, “will go to our mission.”

title: African high school students explore Vermont through a leadership program and cultural exchange
description:
Project Harmony International’s Youth Ambassadors Africa Program hosts 65 students and 10 mentors from Africa in Vermont from July 10 to July 28.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  African high school students explore Vermont through a leadership program and cultural exchange.
text:
A group of Youth Ambassadors from several African countries tours the University of Vermont campus in Burlington on Monday, July 13, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell
When 17-year-old Darius Niyonkuru from Rwanda first heard he was accepted into an international exchange program and was coming to the U.S. for three weeks, he almost didn’t believe it. 
It wasn’t until he received his visa that he realized his dream of coming to America was finally coming true. 
“I wanted to study abroad here even for one day, and then I saw three weeks and I thought, ‘This is impossible,’” he said. 
Niyonkuru was one of 65 high school students staying in Vermont as part of the Youth Ambassadors Africa Program by Project Harmony International, a Waitsfield-based organization that runs exchange programs worldwide. 
From July 8-July 28, the program is bringing students and mentors from 10 countries across sub-Saharan Africa to four different parts of the U.S.: Washington, D.C., Vermont, Alabama and New York. To account for one of the largest groups the organization has seen, the 65 students and 10 mentors were split up into three rotating groups, with each group starting in a different location. 
The first group of students made their way to Vermont July 10 for their six-day stay. While they were here, the students participated in activities intended to facilitate leadership development, entrepreneurial skills and a sense of community in the U.S. 
“These young people are between the ages of 15 and 18, so they’re at the end of their high school career and thinking about what’s next,” said Meg Harris, executive director of PH International. “This provides a good introduction and gives them a good sense of the world, specifically the U.S., and how they might play an important role in it.” 
In early 2025, U.S. foreign assistance was cut by over $8 billion with the systematic dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development, more familiarly known as USAID. Previously funded by USAID, Harris said PH International had lost an estimate of $6 million for selective programs, among other program suspensions. 
Despite the cuts, however, PH International is still able to run their foreign exchange programs through exclusive funding from the U.S. State Department’s Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, Harris said.   
Jennifer Plante, program director for the Youth Ambassadors Africa Program, said the programs are necessary to encourage foreign education on both the academic and cultural level.
“I think when people can talk face to face from different parts of the world, or even different parts of the country, it’s a good thing to just show people what they have in common and what they can agree upon,” Plante said.
For 16-year-old Mariah Lissa Meme from Seychelles, being exposed to new cultures and ways of life was a major factor for doing the program. 
“I wanted to experience something new and meet new people, and just get out of where I was,” Meme said.
A taste for the Green Mountain State 
Throughout their stay, the students toured the Statehouse, visited Vermont Public, tasted local cider from Cold Hollow Cider Mill and partook in a beloved Vermont tradition — trying their first maple creemee. 
But for Meme, the people were the most memorable part of Vermont. She emphasized the “welcoming” nature of the state, a switch from what she is accustomed to back home. 
“Here people mind their business while being nice,” she said. “But in my country, you mind your business and you are rude.” 
Amicha Malano, an 18-year-old student from Guinea, agreed, saying she was in awe of the tight-knit communities in Vermont.
“I like how everybody comes together to make their community grow,” Malano said. “Whether they’re children, teenagers, grown-ups or the elderly, all of them come together and they all have a word to say. It’s not just about the leaders, and that’s really good.” 
Families from Jericho to Salisbury hosted two or three students each as part of the program’s cultural immersion. Harris said the outreach to find the families was mainly done through Front Porch Forum and contacting families that had previously hosted students in the past. 
“We don’t provide any funding or any incentive for them to do it,” she said. “They truly want to be able to show these young people what it’s like in Vermont.” 
One host family from Middlebury, Liz Murino and John Nordmeyer, found their way into the program when they hosted students from Russia in 2016. 
Now, for the first week of the Africa program, Murino and Nordmeyer hosted three students: Claudia June from South Africa, Ashanti Lindiwe from Mozambique and Liza Belinda from Rwanda. 
“We raised three daughters … so it was reminding us what it was like to have our daughters around,” Murino said. 
Murino and Nordmeyer took the three girls to a farmers market in Middlebury, Bartlett Falls swimming hole, a World Cup watch party and Joe’s 19th Hole in Pittsford, where the students indulged in their first creemee.
Murino and Nordmeyer joked that part of their weekend went off script, however, when the girls were eager to tag along with the boy students to a car show in Rutland. 
“What we learned is that teenagers are the same everywhere,” Murino said.
After saying goodbye to the students they hosted for a week, Murino and Nordmeyer said they felt the students had left behind pieces of their cultures just as much as Vermont had left an impression on them. 
The family recalled a time when chaperoning the group at an outdoor funk concert in Ripton turned into an uncommon, surreal sight for Vermont. 
During the concert, at the center of the crowd, the students formed a circle and began doing an African dance, causing the other concertgoers to cheer them on. 
Nordmeyer said the night was a moment he hoped the students would take with them when they left, because it would live on with him for a long time.  
“The whole rest of the audience was just watching this multicultural display that they weren’t particularly expecting in Ripton,” he said. “So they extended out from not just their cultural experience or our cultural experience, but also became part of the whole community.”
